17. !python -m clrs.examples.run --train_steps 10000 --algorithms dfs --hint_mode none --results_df True --save_df True --save_model_to_file True --NSE 25 --filename fifth16 --test_length 16

31. Tips navigating CLRS
32. - Use an editor that quickly lets you find a function's definition with a keyboard shortcut, otherwise tracing prediction through baselines, nets, etc... is time consuming
33. - `run.py` sets up `samplers` which make problem instances (e.g. graphs for DFS).
34.   - problem instances live inside named tuples:
35.     - inputs in `feedback.features.inputs` (e.g. Adjacency matrix and Start node)
36.     - labels inside `feedback.features.outputs` (e.g. Correct DFS tree)
37.     - hints inside `feedback.features.hints` 
38. 
39. - Networks predict on `feedback.features.inputs`

49. 
50. # The CLRS Algorithmic Reasoning Benchmark
51. 
52. Learning representations of algorithms is an emerging area of machine learning,
53. seeking to bridge concepts from neural networks with classical algorithms. The
54. CLRS Algorithmic Reasoning Benchmark (CLRS) consolidates and extends previous
55. work toward evaluation algorithmic reasoning by providing a suite of
56. implementations of classical algorithms. These algorithms have been selected
57. from the third edition of the standard *Introduction to Algorithms* by Cormen,
58. Leiserson, Rivest and Stein.
59. 
60. ## Getting started
61. 
62. The CLRS Algorithmic Reasoning Benchmark can be installed with pip, either from
63. PyPI:
64. 
65. ```shell
66. pip install dm-clrs
67. ```
68. 
69. or directly from GitHub (updated more frequently):
70. 
71. ```shell
72. pip install git+git://github.com/deepmind/clrs.git
73. ```
74. 
75. You may prefer to install it in a virtual environment if any requirements
76. clash with your Python installation:
77. 
78. ```shell
79. python3 -m venv clrs_env
80. source clrs_env/bin/activate
81. pip install git+git://github.com/deepmind/clrs.git
82. ```
83. 
84. Once installed you can run our example baseline model:
85. 
86. ```shell
87. python3 -m clrs.examples.run
88. ```
89. 
90. If this is the first run of the example, the dataset will be downloaded and
91. stored in `--dataset_path` (default '/tmp/CLRS30').
92. Alternatively, you can also download and extract https://storage.googleapis.com/dm-clrs/CLRS30_v1.0.0.tar.gz
93. 
94. ## Algorithms as graphs
95. 
96. CLRS implements the selected algorithms in an idiomatic way, which aligns as
97. closely as possible to the original CLRS 3ed pseudocode. By controlling the
98. input data distribution to conform to the preconditions we are able to
99. automatically generate input/output pairs. We additionally provide trajectories
100. of "hints" that expose the internal state of each algorithm, to both optionally
101. simplify the learning challenge and to distinguish between different algorithms
102. that solve the same overall task (e.g. sorting).
103. 
104. In the most generic sense, algorithms can be seen as manipulating sets of
105. objects, along with any relations between them (which can themselves be
106. decomposed into binary relations). Accordingly, we study all of the algorithms
107. in this benchmark using a graph representation. In the event that objects obey a
108. more strict ordered structure (e.g. arrays or rooted trees), we impose this
109. ordering through inclusion of predecessor links.
110. 
111. ## How it works
112. 
113. For each algorithm, we provide a canonical set of *train*, *eval* and *test*
114. trajectories for benchmarking out-of-distribution generalization.
115. 
116. |       | Trajectories    | Problem Size |
117. |-------|-----------------|--------------|
118. | Train | 1000            | 16           |
119. | Eval  | 32 x multiplier | 16           |
120. | Test  | 32 x multiplier | 64           |
121. 
122. 
123. Here, "problem size" refers to e.g. the length of an array or number of nodes in
124. a graph, depending on the algorithm. "multiplier" is an algorithm-specific
125. factor that increases the number of available *eval* and *test* trajectories
126. to compensate for paucity of evaluation signals. "multiplier" is 1 for all
127. algorithms except:
128. 
129. - Maximum subarray (Kadane), for which "multiplier" is 32.
130. - Quick select, minimum, binary search, string matchers (both naive and KMP),
131. and segment intersection, for which "multiplier" is 64.
132. 
133. The trajectories can be used like so:
134. 
135. ```python
136. train_ds, num_samples, spec = clrs.create_dataset(
137.       folder='/tmp/CLRS30', algorithm='bfs',
138.       split='train', batch_size=32)
139. 
140. for i, feedback in enumerate(train_ds.as_numpy_iterator()):
141.   if i == 0:
142.     model.init(feedback.features, initial_seed)
143.   loss = model.feedback(rng_key, feedback)
144. ```
145. 
146. Here, `feedback` is a `namedtuple` with the following structure:
147. 
148. ```python
149. Feedback = collections.namedtuple('Feedback', ['features', 'outputs'])
150. Features = collections.namedtuple('Features', ['inputs', 'hints', 'lengths'])
151. ```
152. 
153. where the content of `Features` can be used for training and `outputs` is
154. reserved for evaluation. Each field of the tuple is an `ndarray` with a leading
155. batch dimension. Because `hints` are provided for the full algorithm trajectory,
156. these contain an additional time dimension padded up to the maximum length
157. `max(T)` of any trajectory within the dataset. The `lengths` field specifies the
158. true length `t <= max(T)` for each trajectory, which can be used e.g. for loss
159. masking.
160. 
161. The `examples` directory contains a full working Graph Neural Network (GNN)
162. example using JAX and the DeepMind JAX Ecosystem of libraries. It allows
163. training of multiple algorithms on a single processor, as described in
164. ["A Generalist Neural Algorithmic Learner"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.11142).
165. 
166. ## What we provide
167. 
168. ### Algorithms
169. 
170. Our initial CLRS-30 benchmark includes the following 30 algorithms. We aim to
171. support more algorithms in the future.
172. 
173. - Sorting
174.   - Insertion sort
175.   - Bubble sort
176.   - Heapsort (Williams, 1964)
177.   - Quicksort (Hoare, 1962)
178. - Searching
179.   - Minimum
180.   - Binary search
181.   - Quickselect (Hoare, 1961)
182. - Divide and conquer
183.   - Maximum subarray (Kadane's variant) (Bentley, 1984)
184. - Greedy
185.   - Activity selection (Gavril, 1972)
186.   - Task scheduling (Lawler, 1985)
187. - Dynamic programming
188.   - Matrix chain multiplication
189.   - Longest common subsequence
190.   - Optimal binary search tree (Aho et al., 1974)
191. - Graphs
192.   - Depth-first search (Moore, 1959)
193.   - Breadth-first search (Moore, 1959)
194.   - Topological sorting (Knuth, 1973)
195.   - Articulation points
196.   - Bridges
197.   - Kosaraju's strongly connected components algorithm (Aho et al., 1974)
198.   - Kruskal's minimum spanning tree algorithm (Kruskal, 1956)
199.   - Prim's minimum spanning tree algorithm (Prim, 1957)
200.   - Bellman-Ford algorithm for single-source shortest paths (Bellman, 1958)
201.   - Dijkstra's algorithm for single-source shortest paths (Dijkstra et al., 1959)
202.   - Directed acyclic graph single-source shortest paths
203.   - Floyd-Warshall algorithm for all-pairs shortest-paths (Floyd, 1962)
204. - Strings
205.   - Naïve string matching
206.   - Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) string matcher (Knuth et al., 1977)
207. - Geometry
208.   - Segment intersection
209.   - Graham scan convex hull algorithm (Graham, 1972)
210.   - Jarvis' march convex hull algorithm (Jarvis, 1973)
211. 
212. ### Baselines
213. 
214. Models consist of a *processor* and a number of *encoders* and *decoders*.
215. We provide JAX implementations of the following GNN baseline processors:
216. 
217. - Deep Sets (Zaheer et al., NIPS 2017)
218. - End-to-End Memory Networks (Sukhbaatar et al., NIPS 2015)
219. - Graph Attention Networks (Veličković et al., ICLR 2018)
220. - Graph Attention Networks v2 (Brody et al., ICLR 2022)
221. - Message-Passing Neural Networks (Gilmer et al., ICML 2017)
222. - Pointer Graph Networks (Veličković et al., NeurIPS 2020)
223. 
224. If you want to implement a new processor, the easiest way is to add
225. it in the `processors.py` file and make it available through the
226. `get_processor_factory` method there. A processor should have a `__call__`
227. method like this:
228. 
229. ```
230. __call__(self,
231.          node_fts, edge_fts, graph_fts,
232.          adj_mat, hidden,
233.          nb_nodes, batch_size)
234. ```
235. 
236. where `node_fts`, `edge_fts` and `graph_fts` will be float arrays of shape
237. `batch_size` x `nb_nodes` x H, `batch_size` x `nb_nodes` x `nb_nodes` x H,
238. and `batch_size` x H with encoded features for
239. nodes, edges and graph respectively, `adj_mat` a
240. `batch_size` x `nb_nodes` x `nb_nodes` boolean
241. array of connectivity built from hints and inputs, and `hidden` a
242. `batch_size` x `nb_nodes` x H float array with the previous-step outputs
243. of the processor. The method should return a `batch_size` x `nb_nodes` x H
244. float array.
245. 
246. For more fundamentally different baselines, it is necessary to create a new
247. class that extends the Model API (as found within `clrs/_src/model.py`).
248. `clrs/_src/baselines.py` provides one example of how this can be done.
249. 
250. ## Creating your own dataset
251. 
252. We provide a `tensorflow_dataset` generator class in `dataset.py`. This file can
253. be modified to generate different versions of the available algorithms, and it
254. can be built by using `tfds build` after following the installation instructions
255. at https://www.tensorflow.org/datasets.
256. 
257. Alternatively, you can generate samples without going through `tfds` by
258. instantiating samplers with the `build_sampler` method in
259. `clrs/_src/samplers.py`, like so:
260. 
261. ```
262. sampler, spec = clrs.build_sampler(
263.     name='bfs',
264.     seed=42,
265.     num_samples=1000,
266.     length=16)
267. 
268. def _iterate_sampler(batch_size):
269.   while True:
270.     yield sampler.next(batch_size)
271. 
272. for feedback in _iterate_sampler(batch_size=32):
273.   ...
274. 
275. ```
276. 
277. ## Adding new algorithms
278. 
279. Adding a new algorithm to the task suite requires the following steps:
280. 
281. 1. Determine the input/hint/output specification of your algorithm, and include
282. it within the `SPECS` dictionary of `clrs/_src/specs.py`.
283. 2. Implement the desired algorithm in an abstractified form. Examples of this
284. can be found throughout the `clrs/_src/algorithms/` folder.
285.   - Choose appropriate moments within the algorithm’s execution to create probes
286.     that capture the inputs, outputs and all intermediate state (using
287.     the `probing.push` function).
288.   - Once generated, probes must be formatted using the `probing.finalize`
289.     method, and should be returned together with the algorithm output.
290. 3. Implement an appropriate input data sampler for your algorithm,
291. and include it in the `SAMPLERS` dictionary within `clrs/_src/samplers.py`.
292. 
293. Once the algorithm has been added in this way, it can be accessed with the
294. `build_sampler` method, and will also be incorporated to the dataset if
295. regenerated with the generator class in `dataset.py`, as described above.
296. 
297. ## Citation
298. 
299. To cite the CLRS Algorithmic Reasoning Benchmark:
300. 
301. ```latex
302. @article{deepmind2022clrs,
303.   title={The CLRS Algorithmic Reasoning Benchmark},
304.   author={Petar Veli\v{c}kovi\'{c} and Adri\`{a} Puigdom\`{e}nech Badia and
305.     David Budden and Razvan Pascanu and Andrea Banino and Misha Dashevskiy and
306.     Raia Hadsell and Charles Blundell},
307.   journal={arXiv preprint arXiv:2205.15659},
308.   year={2022}
309. }
310. ```
311.
````

65. def single_sample_upwards(probMatrix):
66.     '''copy-pasted brain from def sample_upwards'''
67.     probMatrix = np.array(probMatrix)  # deepcopy to numpy so mutable
68. 
69.     # sort by leafiness
70.     leafiness = np.asarray(leafinessSort(probMatrix))  # shallowcopy jax array to numpy array so no problems indexing
71. 
72.     # grab most leafy, find its parent, continue till already-discovered (self-parent or prev. iter).
73.     pi = np.full(len(probMatrix), np.inf)
74.     while sum(leafiness) > -len(leafiness):
75.         altered_ProbMatrix = rowWiseProb(probMatrix)
76.         leaf = leafiness[leafiness != -1][0]
77.         # sample the leafs parent
78.         parent = chooseUniformly(altered_ProbMatrix[leaf])
79.         pi[leaf] = parent  # FIXME sometimes index error
80.         leafiness[leaf] = -1
81.         leafiness[parent] = -1
82.         altered_ProbMatrix[:,leaf] = 0  # set leaf's column to 0: leaf should be nobody's parent, unless there's a restart, to avoid cycles... BREAKS
83. 
84.         # sample up the tree until parent is the start node, a self-loop or already has a parent
85.         while pi[parent] == np.inf:
86.             # sample up the tree
87.             leaf = parent
88.             parent = chooseUniformly(altered_ProbMatrix[leaf])
89.             pi[leaf] = parent
90.             # remove parent as potential
91.             leafiness[leaf] = -1
92.             leafiness[parent] = -1
93.             altered_ProbMatrix[:,leaf] = 0  # set leaf's column to 0: leaf should be nobody's parent, unless there's a restart, to avoid cycles
94. 
95.     if sum(np.isin(pi, np.inf)) > 0:
96.         raise ValueError("Leaf with no parent")
97. 
98.     return pi

102. def sample_upwards(outsOrPreds):
103.     '''
104. 
105.     Args:
106.         outsOrPreds: A list of Datapoint or Dictionaries containing JaxArray Probability Matrices
107. 
108.     Returns:
109.         trees: A list of parent trees, one for each probability Matrix in unpacked outsOrPreds.

114.         probMatrix: A matrix, #nodes by #nodes, where probMatrix[i][j] indicates the probability that node j is the parent of node i.

117.     '''

127.             probMatrix = np.array(probMatrix) # deepcopy to numpy so mutable
128.             ### COMPUTATION HERE
129.             #. sort by leafiness
130.             leafiness = np.asarray(leafinessSort(probMatrix)) # shallowcopy jax array to numpy array so no problems indexing
131. 
132.             # turn probmatrix into true probability dist (summing to 1)
133.             #altered_ProbMatrix= probMatrix
134.             #. grab most leafy, find its parent, continue till already-discovered (self-parent or prev. iter).
135.             pi = np.full(len(probMatrix), np.inf)

141.                 pi[leaf] = parent # FIXME sometimes index error

145. 
146.                 # sample up the tree until parent is the start node, a self-loop or already has a parent
147.                 while pi[parent] == np.inf:

151.                     pi[leaf] = parent

154.                     leafiness[parent] = -1
155.                     altered_ProbMatrix[:, leaf] = 0 # set leaf's column to 0: leaf should be nobody's parent, unless there's a restart, to avoid cycles
156. 
157.             if sum(np.isin(pi, np.inf)) > 0:
158.                 raise ValueError("Leaf with no parent")

162. def leafinessSort(probMatrix):
163.     '''
164.     Args:
165.         probMatrix: Expects probMatrix[i][j] to indicate the probability that node j is the parent of node i
166. 
167.     Returns: sorted-list of vertex indices where first node had lowest probability of being parent. (column with lowest sum).
168.     '''
169.     sums = np.sum(probMatrix, axis=0)
170.     # sort by sum column, remember the original column number
171.     leafiness = np.argsort(sums)
172.     return leafiness
173. 
174. def rowWiseProb(probMatrix):
175.     for row_ix in range(len(probMatrix)):
176.         if probMatrix[row_ix].sum() != 0:
177.             probMatrix[row_ix] = probMatrix[row_ix].astype(np.float64)/probMatrix[row_ix].astype(np.float64).sum()
178.     return probMatrix
179. 
180. 
181. # -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
182. # SHARED HELPERS
183. # -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
184. 
185. def extract_probMatrices(outsOrPreds):
186.     ''''
187.     handles ugly formatting difference: outs a list of dicts of datapoints,
188.     preds a list of datapoints
189.     '''
190.     # what special here about preds/outputs different from list of npArrays which misbehave
191.     big_probmatrix_list = []
192.     for i in outsOrPreds:
193.         if type(i) == type({}):
194.             distlist = i["pi"].data
195.         else:
196.             distlist = i.data
197.         big_probmatrix_list.extend(distlist)
198.     #breakpoint()
199.     return big_probmatrix_list
200. 
201. def chooseUniformly(notProbArray):
202.     '''Expects notProbArray'''
203.     val = np.random.uniform(low=0, high=sum(notProbArray))
204.     sums = np.cumsum(notProbArray)
205.     for threshold_ix in range(len(sums)):
206.         if val < sums[threshold_ix]:
207.             return threshold_ix
208.     return np.random.randint(len(notProbArray))
209. 
210. # -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
211. # ALTUPWARDS
212. # -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
213. def sample_altUpwards(outsOrPreds):
214.     # search up
215.     probMatrix_list = extract_probMatrices(outsOrPreds)
216.     pi_trees = []
217.     for probMatrix in probMatrix_list:
218.         # build a pi-tree, sampling up
219.         pi_trees.append(get_parent_tree_upwards(probMatrix))
220.     return pi_trees
221. 
222. def get_parent_tree_upwards(probMatrix):
223.     '''according to leafiness, explore upwards, until all nodes have parents (could be themselves)'''
224.     parent_guesses = np.full(len(probMatrix), np.inf)
225.     leafiness = leafinessSort(probMatrix)  # most leafy is least-likely to be a parent: lowest column sum of probMatrix
226.     for node_ix in leafiness:
227.         if parent_guesses[node_ix] == np.inf:
228.             parent_guesses = explore_upwards(node_ix, parent_guesses, probMatrix)
229.     if np.inf in parent_guesses:
230.         raise ValueError('not guessing parent for someone')
231.     return parent_guesses
232. 
233. def explore_upwards(orphan_ix, parent_guesses, probMatrix):
234.     '''starting at node_ix, sample parents upwards until you find a node which already has a parent'''
235.     while parent_guesses[orphan_ix] == np.inf: # until you find node who already has parent,
236.         # sample parent according to row of notExactlyProbs
237.         parent_guess = chooseUniformly(probMatrix[orphan_ix])
238.         parent_guesses[orphan_ix] = parent_guess
239.         # try further up the tree
240.         orphan_ix = parent_guess
241.     return parent_guesses
242.

4. def sample_bfs_prim(outsOrPreds, s_indices):
5.     """
6.     Samples BFS trees using a Prim-like greedy approach.
7.     
8.     Args:
9.         outsOrPreds: Model outputs containing parent probabilities.
10.         s_indices: List of source node indices for each graph in the batch.
11.         
12.     Returns:
13.         List of parent arrays (pi), one for each graph in the batch.
14.     """
15.     probMatrix_list = dfs_sampling.extract_probMatrices(outsOrPreds)
16.     pi_trees = []
17.     
18.     # Handle case where s_indices might be a single int or list
19.     if isinstance(s_indices, int):
20.         s_indices = [s_indices] * len(probMatrix_list)
21.         
22.     for i, probMatrix in enumerate(probMatrix_list):
23.         s = s_indices[i]
24.         pi = prim_like_sampler(probMatrix, s)
25.         pi_trees.append(pi)
26.         
27.     return pi_trees

29. def prim_like_sampler(probMatrix, s):
30.     """
31.     Constructs a BFS tree starting from the root, adding nodes that are most likely 
32.     connected to the current tree.
33.     
34.     Args:
35.         probMatrix: N x N matrix where P[i, j] is prob that j is parent of i.
36.         s: Source node index.
37.         
38.     Returns:
39.         pi: Array of length N, where pi[i] is the parent of i.
40.     """
41.     num_nodes = probMatrix.shape[0]
42.     pi = np.full(num_nodes, -1, dtype=int) # -1 indicates not yet processed/no parent
43.     pi[s] = s
44.     
45.     processed = {s}
46.     remaining = set(range(num_nodes)) - {s}
47.     
48.     # To optimize, we could maintain scores, but N is likely small (<= 64 usually in CLRS)
49.     # So recomputing sum might be fast enough.
50.     
51.     while remaining:
52.         best_v = -1
53.         best_score = -1.0
54.         
55.         # Find v in remaining with highest prob of attaching to processed set
56.         # score(v) = sum_{u in processed} P(parent(v) = u)
57.         for v in remaining:
58.             # probMatrix[v, u] is prob that u is parent of v.
59.             # We sum over u in processed.
60.             score = sum(probMatrix[v, u] for u in processed)
61.             
62.             if score > best_score:
63.                 best_score = score
64.                 best_v = v
65.         
66.         if best_v == -1:
67.             # This happens if remaining nodes have 0 prob of connecting to processed nodes
68.             # (disconnected graph components). 
69.             # We just pick one arbitrarily or handle it?
70.             # For BFS, disconnected nodes typically point to themselves or have 0 parent in some representations.
71.             # Here, let's just pick the first one and attach it to itself (or closest processed if any non-zero).
72.             best_v = list(remaining)[0]
73.             # If score is 0, it means no connection.
74.             # We'll just process it to avoid infinite loop.
75.             
76.         # Sample parent for best_v from processed set
77.         # Probabilities are P(parent(best_v) = u) for u in processed
78.         # We need to normalize these to sum to 1.
79.         
80.         candidate_parents = list(processed)
81.         probs = np.array([probMatrix[best_v, u] for u in candidate_parents])
82.         
83.         total_prob = probs.sum()
84.         if total_prob > 0:
85.             probs = probs / total_prob
86.             parent = np.random.choice(candidate_parents, p=probs)
87.         else:
88.             # No valid parent in processed set (disconnected). 
89.             # Default to self-loop or some fallback.
90.             parent = best_v 
91.             
92.         pi[best_v] = parent
93.         processed.add(best_v)
94.         remaining.remove(best_v)
95.         
96.     return pi
97. 
98. def sample_bfs_categorical(outsOrPreds):
99.     """
100.     Samples parent pointers independently for each node using categorical sampling.
101.     Note: This does NOT guarantee a tree structure (may contain cycles or orphans).
102.     
103.     Args:           
104.         outsOrPreds: Model outputs containing parent probabilities.
105.         
106.     Returns:
107.         List of parent arrays (pi).
108.     """
109.     probMatrix_list = dfs_sampling.extract_probMatrices(outsOrPreds)
110.     pi_trees = []
111.     
112.     for probMatrix in probMatrix_list:
113.         num_nodes = probMatrix.shape[0]
114.         pi = np.zeros(num_nodes, dtype=int)
115.         
116.         for i in range(num_nodes):
117.             # Sample parent for node i based on the distribution in row i
118.             probs = probMatrix[i]
119.             # Ensure probabilities sum to 1 for np.random.choice
120.             total_p = np.sum(probs)
121.             assert total_p >= 0, "Probabilities must be non-negative"
122.             if total_p > 0:
123.                 normalized_probs = probs / total_p
124.                 pi[i] = np.random.choice(num_nodes, p=normalized_probs)
125.                 
126.         pi_trees.append(pi)
127.         
128.     return pi_trees

130. def sample_bfs_beam(outsOrPreds, s_indices, beam_width=3):
131.     """
132.     Samples BFS trees using a Beam Search approach.
133.     
134.     Args:
135.         outsOrPreds: Model outputs containing parent probabilities.
136.         s_indices: List of source node indices.
137.         beam_width: Number of hypotheses to keep.
138.         
139.     Returns:
140.         List of parent arrays (pi).
141.     """
142.     probMatrix_list = dfs_sampling.extract_probMatrices(outsOrPreds)
143.     pi_trees = []
144.     
145.     if isinstance(s_indices, int):
146.         s_indices = [s_indices] * len(probMatrix_list)
147.         
148.     for i, probMatrix in enumerate(probMatrix_list):
149.         s = s_indices[i]
150.         pi = bfs_beam_sampler(probMatrix, s, beam_width)
151.         pi_trees.append(pi)
152.         
153.     return pi_trees
154. 
155. def bfs_beam_sampler(probMatrix, s, beam_width):
156.     num_nodes = probMatrix.shape[0]
157.     
158.     # State: (log_prob, pi_array, processed_set_as_tuple)
159.     # processed_set is stored as tuple for hashing/copying if needed, though sets are fine if we copy.
160.     # pi_array initialized with -1
161.     initial_pi = np.full(num_nodes, -1, dtype=int)
162.     initial_pi[s] = s
163.     
164.     # Beam: list of dicts or objects. 
165.     # Let's use a simple dict: {'log_prob': 0.0, 'pi': pi, 'processed': {s}}
166.     beam = [{'log_prob': 0.0, 'pi': initial_pi, 'processed': {s}}]
167.     
168.     # We need to add N-1 nodes
169.     for _ in range(num_nodes - 1):
170.         candidates = []
171.         
172.         for hyp in beam:
173.             processed = hyp['processed']
174.             pi = hyp['pi']
175.             curr_log_prob = hyp['log_prob']
176.             remaining = set(range(num_nodes)) - processed
177.             
178.             if not remaining:
179.                 candidates.append(hyp)
180.                 continue
181.             
182.             # 1. Select next node `v` to add (Greedy heuristic)
183.             # We pick the v with highest total probability of connecting to current processed set
184.             best_v = -1
185.             best_connection_mass = -1.0
186.             
187.             for v in remaining:
188.                 # Sum of probs from processed nodes to v
189.                 # probMatrix[v, u] is P(parent(v)=u)
190.                 mass = sum(probMatrix[v, u] for u in processed)
191.                 if mass > best_connection_mass:
192.                     best_connection_mass = mass
193.                     best_v = v
194.             
195.             if best_v == -1:
196.                 best_v = list(remaining)[0] # Disconnected/fallback
197.                 
198.             # 2. Branch on all possible parents u in processed for best_v
199.             possible_parents = list(processed)
200.             
201.             for u in possible_parents:
202.                 p_val = probMatrix[best_v, u]
203.                 if p_val > 1e-9: # Avoid log(0)
204.                     new_log_prob = curr_log_prob + np.log(p_val)
205.                 else:
206.                     new_log_prob = curr_log_prob - 1e9 # Penalty
207.                 
208.                 new_pi = pi.copy()
209.                 new_pi[best_v] = u
210.                 new_processed = processed.copy()
211.                 new_processed.add(best_v)
212.                 
213.                 candidates.append({
214.                     'log_prob': new_log_prob,
215.                     'pi': new_pi,
216.                     'processed': new_processed
217.                 })
218.         
219.         if not candidates:
220.             break # Should not happen usually unless disconnected
221. 
222.         # Select top-k candidates
223.         # Sort by log_prob descending
224.         candidates.sort(key=lambda x: x['log_prob'], reverse=True)
225.         beam = candidates[:beam_width]
226.         
227.     return beam[0]['pi'] # Return best hypothesis

242. def BFS_multi_collect_and_eval(sampler, predict_fn, sample_count, rng_key, extras, 
243.                                 filename='bfs_accuracy', vd_flag=False, NSE=100):
244.     """Collect batches of output and hint preds and evaluate BFS multi-solution."""
245.     processed_samples = 0
246.     preds = []
247.     outputs = []
248.     As = []
249.     source_nodes = []
250.     
251.     while processed_samples < sample_count:
252.         feedback = next(sampler)
253.         batch_size = feedback.outputs[0].data.shape[0]
254.         outputs.append(feedback.outputs)
255.         new_rng_key, rng_key = jax.random.split(rng_key)
256.         cur_preds, _ = predict_fn(new_rng_key, feedback.features)
257.         preds.append(cur_preds)
258.         processed_samples += batch_size
259.         
260.         # BFS: feedback[0][0][1] is 's' (source), feedback[0][0][2] is 'A' (adjacency)
261.         As.append(feedback[0][0][2].data)
262.         source_nodes.append(np.argmax(feedback[0][0][1].data, axis=1))
263.

267.     preds = _concat(preds, axis=0)
268.     
269.     # Standard CLRS evaluation
270.     out = clrs.evaluate(outputs, preds)
271. 
272.     # === CATEGORICAL SAMPLING ===
273.     model_sample_categorical = bfs_sampling.sample_bfs_categorical([preds])
274.     true_sample_categorical = bfs_sampling.sample_bfs_categorical(outputs)

278.         for i in range(len(model_sample_categorical))
279.     ]

281.

283.         check_graphs.check_valid_bfsTree(As[i], true_sample_categorical[i], s=source_nodes[i]) 
284.         for i in range(len(true_sample_categorical))
285.     ]   
286.     correctness_true_categorical = sum(true_categorical_truthmask) / len(true_categorical_truthmask)
287.     
288.     # === RANDOM SAMPLING ===
289.     model_sample_random = dfs_sampling.sample_random_list([preds])
290.     true_sample_random = dfs_sampling.sample_random_list(outputs)
291.     
292.     model_random_truthmask = [
293.         check_graphs.check_valid_bfsTree(As[i], model_sample_random[i], s=source_nodes[i]) 
294.         for i in range(len(model_sample_random))
295.     ]
296.     correctness_model_random = sum(model_random_truthmask) / len(model_random_truthmask)
297.     
298.     true_random_truthmask = [
299.         check_graphs.check_valid_bfsTree(As[i], true_sample_random[i], s=source_nodes[i]) 
300.         for i in range(len(true_sample_random))
301.     ]
302.     correctness_true_random = sum(true_random_truthmask) / len(true_random_truthmask)
303.     
304.     # === PRIM-LIKE SAMPLING (BFS-specific) ===
305.     model_sample_prim = bfs_sampling.sample_bfs_prim([preds], source_nodes)
306.     true_sample_prim = bfs_sampling.sample_bfs_prim(outputs, source_nodes)
307.     
308.     model_prim_truthmask = [
309.         check_graphs.check_valid_bfsTree(As[i], model_sample_prim[i], s=source_nodes[i])
310.         for i in range(len(model_sample_prim))
311.     ]
312.     correctness_model_prim = sum(model_prim_truthmask) / len(model_prim_truthmask)
313.     
314.     true_prim_truthmask = [
315.         check_graphs.check_valid_bfsTree(As[i], true_sample_prim[i], s=source_nodes[i])
316.         for i in range(len(true_sample_prim))
317.     ]
318.     correctness_true_prim = sum(true_prim_truthmask) / len(true_prim_truthmask)
319.     
320.     # === BEAM SEARCH SAMPLING (BFS-specific) ===
321.     model_sample_beam = bfs_sampling.sample_bfs_beam([preds], source_nodes, beam_width=3)
322.     true_sample_beam = bfs_sampling.sample_bfs_beam(outputs, source_nodes, beam_width=3)
323.     
324.     model_beam_truthmask = [
325.         check_graphs.check_valid_bfsTree(As[i], model_sample_beam[i], s=source_nodes[i])
326.         for i in range(len(model_sample_beam))
327.     ]
328.     correctness_model_beam = sum(model_beam_truthmask) / len(model_beam_truthmask)
329.     
330.     true_beam_truthmask = [
331.         check_graphs.check_valid_bfsTree(As[i], true_sample_beam[i], s=source_nodes[i])
332.         for i in range(len(true_sample_beam))
333.     ]
334.     correctness_true_beam = sum(true_beam_truthmask) / len(true_beam_truthmask)
335. 
336.     
337.     # === LOGGING ===
338.     As_flat = [i.flatten() for i in As]
339.     result_dict = {
340.         "As": As_flat,

342.         #

349.         #

353.         "Random_True_Mask": true_random_truthmask,
354.         "Random_Model_Accuracy": correctness_model_random,
355.         "Random_True_Accuracy": correctness_true_random,
356.         #
357.         "Prim_Model_Trees": model_sample_prim,
358.         "Prim_True_Trees": true_sample_prim,
359.         "Prim_Model_Mask": model_prim_truthmask,
360.         "Prim_True_Mask": true_prim_truthmask,
361.         "Prim_Model_Accuracy": correctness_model_prim,
362.         "Prim_True_Accuracy": correctness_true_prim,
363.         #

367.         "Beam_True_Mask": true_beam_truthmask,

369.         "Beam_True_Accuracy": correctness_true_beam,
370.     }
371.     save_results(result_dict, f"{filename}_BFS")
372.     
373.     if extras:
374.         out.update(extras)
375.     return {k: unpack(v) for k, v in out.items()}

382. def DFS_collect_and_eval(sampler, predict_fn, sample_count, rng_key, extras, filename = 'dfs_accuracy', vd_flag=False, NSE = 100):
383.     """Collect batch of output preds and evaluate them."""
384.     processed_samples = 0

393.         cur_preds, _ = predict_fn(new_rng_key, feedback.features)
394.         preds.append(cur_preds)
395.         processed_samples += batch_size
396.         As.append(feedback[0][0][1].data)

407.         outputs_vd[0].data = outputs_vd[0].data[:10]
408.         preds_vd[0]['pi'].data = preds_vd[0]['pi'].data[:10]
409.         dataframes, _, _ = validate_distributions(As=As_vd, Ss=[0]*len(As_vd), outsOrPreds=preds_vd,
410.                                             numSolsExtracting=NSE, flag='DFS')  # note not wrapping preds in list for extract_probmatrices to work
411.         #breakpoint()

413.         df, _, _ = validate_distributions(As=As_vd, Ss=[0]*len(As_vd), outsOrPreds=preds_vd, numSolsExtracting=NSE, edge_reuse_DFS=True, flag = "dummy")
414. 
415.         # plot_edge_reuse_matrix_list_median(df, len(As[0]))
416.         # breakpoint()
417.         plot_edge_reuse_matrix_list_mean_dfs(df, len(As[0]))
418.         line_plot_dfs(df, len(As[0]))

421.     # 1. Sample from preds a candidate tree
422.     # 2. run check_graphs on candidate tree (using A as groundtruth)
423.     # 3. Collect validity result into a dataframe.

425.     t1 = time.time()
426.     ##### RANDOM

428.     true_sample_random = dfs_sampling.sample_random_list(outputs)

449.     correctness_true_argmax = sum(true_argmax_truthmask) / len(true_argmax_truthmask)

      self,

      sub_seed = self._rng.randint(0, 2**31)

385. def bfs_multi(A: _Array, s: int, seed: int, deterministic=False) -> _Out:
386.   """Multiple solution breadth-first search."""
387.   rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)
388. 
389.   chex.assert_rank(A, 2)
390.   probeslist = []
391.   pies = []
392. 
393.   if deterministic:
394.     NUM_SOLUTIONS = 1
395.   else: 
396.     NUM_SOLUTIONS = 20
397. 
398.   for i in range(NUM_SOLUTIONS):
399.     probes = probing.initialize(specs.SPECS['bfs_multi'])
400. 
401.     A_pos = np.arange(A.shape[0])
402. 
403.     probing.push(
404.         probes,
405.         specs.Stage.INPUT,
406.         next_probe={
407.             'pos': np.copy(A_pos) * 1.0 / A.shape[0],
408.             's': probing.mask_one(s, A.shape[0]),
409.             'A': np.copy(A),
410.             'adj': probing.graph(np.copy(A))
411.         })
412. 
413.     reach = np.zeros(A.shape[0])
414.     pi = np.arange(A.shape[0])
415.     reach[s] = 1
416.     while True:
417.       prev_reach = np.copy(reach)
418.       probing.push(
419.           probes,
420.           specs.Stage.HINT,
421.           next_probe={
422.               'reach_h': np.copy(prev_reach),
423.               'pi_h': np.copy(pi)
424.           })
425.       
426.       # Randomise order of sources (reached nodes) to generate different valid BFS trees
427.       # All nodes in prev_reach are at the same distance from root, so any can be a valid parent
428.       # Shuffling determines which one "claims" a child first when multiple are valid
429.       n = A.shape[0]
430.       sources = np.where(prev_reach == 1)[0]
431.       if deterministic:
432.         shuffled_sources = sources
433.       else:
434.         shuffled_sources = np.copy(sources)
435.         rng.shuffle(shuffled_sources)
436.       for src in shuffled_sources:
437.         for j in range(n):
438.           if A[src, j] > 0:
439.             if pi[j] == j and j != s:
440.               pi[j] = src
441.             reach[j] = 1
442.       if np.all(reach == prev_reach):
443.         break
444. 
445.     probing.push(probes, specs.Stage.OUTPUT, next_probe={'pi': np.copy(pi)})
446.     probing.finalize(probes)
447. 
448.     pies.append(pi)
449.     probeslist.append(probes)
450. 
451.   ### copied from DFS CODE
452.   # build adj matrix of "is i a parent of j in any pi", sums and divides.
453.   adjs = []
454.   for i in range(NUM_SOLUTIONS):
455.       adj = np.zeros(A.shape)
456.       for j in range(len(pies[0])):  # what's the parent of j?
457.           #breakpoint()
458.           adj[j, pies[i][j]] = 1  # at row j, put 1 in the column corresponding to parent
459.       adjs.append(adj)
460.   parent_dist = sum(adjs) / NUM_SOLUTIONS
461.   # parent_dist = sp.special.logit(parent_dist)
462.   # print(probes)
463.   # print(parent_dist)
464.   probeslist[0]['output']['node']['pi']['data'] = parent_dist
465. 
466.   #breakpoint()
467.   ## CHECK THE PUSHING!
468.   return parent_dist, probeslist[0]

def parent_tree_to_adj_matrix(tree):
    size = len(tree)    # n_vertices
    M = np.zeros((size, size))
    for ix in range(size):
        M[int(tree[ix]), ix] = 1     # edge points tree[ix] to ix, bcuz parent tree
    return M

def no_self_loops_parent_tree_to_adj_matrix(tree):
    """now root is just any node without parent"""
    M = parent_tree_to_adj_matrix(tree)
    np.fill_diagonal(a=M, val=0)
    return M

def adj_matrix_to_parent_tree(A):
    size = len(A)
    tree = np.zeros(size)
    for i in range(size):
        for j in range(size):
            if A[i,j] == 1:
                tree[j] = i
    return tree

def _maybe_pick_first_pmapped(tree):
  if jax.local_device_count() == 1:
    return tree
  return jax.tree_util.tree_map(lambda x: x[0], tree)


@jax.jit
def _restack_from_pmap(tree):
  """Stack the results of a pmapped computation across the first two axes."""
  restack_array = lambda x: jnp.reshape(x, (-1,) + x.shape[2:])
  return jax.tree_util.tree_map(restack_array, tree)


def _maybe_restack_from_pmap(tree):
  if jax.local_device_count() == 1:
    return tree
  return _restack_from_pmap(tree)


@functools.partial(jax.jit, static_argnums=[1, 2])
def _pmap_reshape(x, n_devices, split_axis=0):
  """Splits a pytree over n_devices on axis split_axis for pmapping."""
  def _reshape(arr):
    new_shape = (arr.shape[:split_axis] +
                 (n_devices, arr.shape[split_axis] // n_devices) +
                 arr.shape[split_axis + 1:])
    return jnp.moveaxis(jnp.reshape(arr, new_shape), split_axis, 0)
  return jax.tree_util.tree_map(_reshape, x)


def _maybe_pmap_reshape(x, split_axis=0):
  n_devices = jax.local_device_count()
  if n_devices == 1:
    return x
  return _pmap_reshape(x, n_devices, split_axis)

def _pmap_data(data: Union[_Feedback, _Features], n_devices: int):

new_spec[k] = spec[k]

  return new_spec, _iterate()


def process_random_pos(sample_iterator, rng):
  """Randomize the `pos` input from a sampler.

  The `pos` input is, by default, a scalar uniformly spaced between 0 and 1
  across the nodes. The exception are string algorithms (naive_string_matcher,
  kmp_string_matcher and lcs_length), where the `pos` sequence is split into
  needle and haystack (or first and second string, for lcs_length). Here
  we replace the uniformly spaced `pos` with an ordered sequence of random
  scalars, or, for string algorithms, two ordered sequences of random scalars.

  Args:
    sample_iterator: An iterator producing samples with non-random `pos` inputs.
    rng: Numpy random generator
  Returns:
    An iterator returning the samples with randomized `pos` inputs.
  """
  def _iterate():
    while True:
      feedback = next(sample_iterator)
      inputs = feedback.features.inputs
      pos, = [x for x in inputs if x.name == 'pos']
      batch_size, num_nodes = pos.data.shape
      unsorted = rng.uniform(size=(batch_size, num_nodes))
      new_pos = []
      for i in range(batch_size):  # we check one example at a time.
        # We find if there are splits in the pos sequence, marked by zeros.
        # We know there will always be at least 1 zero, if there's no split.
        split, = np.where(pos.data[i] == 0)
        split = np.concatenate([split, [num_nodes]])
        # We construct the randomized pos by sorting the random values in each
        # split and concatenating them.
        new_pos.append(
            np.concatenate([np.sort(unsorted[i, split[j]:split[j+1]])
                            for j in range(len(split) - 1)]))
      pos.data = np.array(new_pos)
      inputs = [(pos if x.name == 'pos' else x) for x in inputs]
      features = feedback.features._replace(inputs=inputs)
      feedback = feedback._replace(features=features)
      yield feedback

  return _iterate()

import numpy as np
import clrs._src.dfs_sampling as dfs_sampling
import clrs._src.algorithms.check_graphs as check_graphs
from clrs._src.algorithms.BF_beamsearch import sample_beamsearch


def check_uniqueness_dfs(As, probMatrices, n_samples = 5, method = "upwards"):
    uniques = []
    valids_uniques = []
    valids = []

    # issue: we are getting back list of trees from sample upwards, so we need to merge those in a way where
    # every index corresponds to the probmatrix we are sampling from
    #breakpoint()
    if method == "upwards":
        samples = np.array([dfs_sampling.sample_upwards(probMatrices) for j in range(n_samples)])
    elif method == "altupwards":
        samples = np.array([dfs_sampling.sample_altUpwards(probMatrices) for j in range(n_samples)])
    else:
        raise ValueError("Invalid Upwards Sampling method")
    probMatrices_format = dfs_sampling.extract_probMatrices(probMatrices)
    for i in range(len(probMatrices_format)):

        samples_matrix_i = samples[:,i] # first tree from each run, corresponds to n_samples runs on first graph

        # code from here: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/26514179/set-of-list-of-lists-in-python
        unique_trees = [list(item) for item in set([tuple(row) for row in samples_matrix_i])]

        #breakpoint()
        # save the fraction of unique samples
        uniques.append(len(unique_trees)/n_samples)

        valid_trees_of_uniques = [check_graphs.check_valid_dfsTree(As[i],j) for j in unique_trees]
        valids_uniques.append(sum(valid_trees_of_uniques)/len(unique_trees))

        valid_trees= [check_graphs.check_valid_dfsTree(As[i], j) for j in samples_matrix_i]
        valids.append(sum(valid_trees) / n_samples)
        #breakpoint()

    return uniques,valids_uniques, valids

## COMPREHENSIVE ARCHITECTURE ANALYSIS: CLRS Multi-Solution NAR Framework

---

## **SECTION A: Repository Architecture Summary**

### Overall Structure
**Root-level project**: Neural Algorithmic Reasoning framework extended to handle **multiple correct solutions** for underdetermined algorithms (DFS, BFS, Bellman-Ford). Built on DeepMind's CLRS-30 benchmark baseline.

**Directory Layout**:
- `/clrs/_src/` — Core algorithmic reasoning source (BASE + CUSTOM)
  - `algorithms/` — Algorithm implementations (DFS, BFS, etc.) with multi-solution variants
  - `samplers.py` — Dataset generation & algorithm selection (710+ lines; contains DfsMultiSampler, BfsMultiSampler)
  - `baselines.py` — GNN baseline models (JAX/Haiku; 799 lines)
  - `processors.py` — Graph neural network architectures (914 lines)
  - `nets.py` — Model layer definitions (719 lines)
  - `model.py` — Abstract Model API
  - `encoders.py`, `decoders.py` — Input/output encoding layers
  - `losses.py` — Training objectives (including **KL divergence for distribution learning**)
  - `probing.py` — Trajectory recording/debugging infrastructure
  - `specs.py` — Algorithm I/O specifications (570 lines; includes dfs_multi, bfs_multi, bellman_ford_multi)
  - `evaluation.py` — Baseline metrics computation
  - **CUSTOM MULTI-SOLUTION FILES**:
    - `dfs_sampling.py` — **Stochastic solution extraction** (247 lines): sample_upwards, sample_altUpwards, sample_random_list, sample_argmax
    - `bfs_sampling.py` — **BFS tree sampling** (226 lines): sample_bfs_prim, sample_bfs_categorical, sample_bfs_beam
    - `dfs_uniqueness_check.py` — Validity & uniqueness metrics for DFS
    - `bf_uniqueness_check.py` — Validity & uniqueness metrics for Bellman-Ford
    - `validate_distributions.py` — **Core distribution analysis** (914 lines): empirical solution distribution extraction, edge-reuse analysis
    - `test_rerunning_number/` — Experimental utilities for multi-run generation

- `/clrs/examples/` — Training & evaluation pipelines
  - `run.py` — **Main training loop** (644 lines); flags: `--NSE` (NumSolutionsExtracted), `--algorithms dfs_multi/bfs_multi`
  - `log_experiments.py` — **Evaluation functions** (557 lines):
    - `DFS_collect_and_eval()` — DFS multi-solution evaluation
    - `BFS_multi_collect_and_eval()` — BFS multi-solution evaluation
    - `BF_collect_and_eval()` — Bellman-Ford evaluation
  - `mod-run.py` — Alternative training entry point
  - `plot.py` — Visualization utilities

- `/results/`, `/clrs_env/` — Outputs, environment

### Key Files Bridging CLRS Baseline → Custom Multi-Solution Logic
| Purpose | Baseline Component | Custom Extension |
|---------|-------------------|------------------|
| **Algorithm Definition** | `algorithms/graphs.py` (e.g., `dfs()`) | `dfs_multi()`, `bfs_multi()` at lines 177, 385 — **Generate 20 solutions per input via random shuffling** |
| **Data Sampling** | `samplers.py`: `DfsSampler`, `BfsSampler` | `DfsMultiSampler` (line 425), `BfsMultiSampler` (line 458) — **Pass seed to algorithm for reproducible multi-runs** |
| **Training Loss** | `losses.py`: MSE, cross-entropy | Line 84 onwards: **KL divergence** (`kl_div()`) for distribution matching |
| **Evaluation** | `clrs.evaluate()` standard metrics | `DFS_collect_and_eval`, `BFS_multi_collect_and_eval` in `log_experiments.py` — **5 sampling methods per algorithm** |
| **Solution Extraction** | N/A | `dfs_sampling.py`, `bfs_sampling.py` — **Stochastic sampling from learned probability distributions** |

---

## **SECTION B: Current Data Pipeline by Stage**

### **STAGE 1: SAMPLING / GENERATION**
**Files**: `clrs/_src/samplers.py` (lines 425-475), `clrs/_src/algorithms/graphs.py`

**For DFS Multi-Solution** (lines 177–343 in graphs.py):
```
Input: Adjacency matrix A, seed
→ DfsMultiSampler generates: [graph, sub_seed]
→ dfs_multi(A, seed, deterministic=False):
    FOR i in range(NUM_SOLUTIONS=20):
        - Initialize probes for timesteps
        - Shuffle node adjacency order (line 214): rng.shuffle(shuffled)
        - Run DFS with randomized neighbor selection (different valid trees)
        - Record pi (parent pointers) for each run
    → Average all 20 pi outputs → parent_dist (n×n empirical distribution)
    → Return: parent_dist, probeslist[0]
```

**For BFS Multi-Solution** (lines 385–468 in graphs.py):
```
Input: Adjacency matrix A, source s, seed
→ BfsMultiSampler generates: [graph, source_node, sub_seed]
→ bfs_multi(A, s, seed, deterministic=False):
    FOR i in range(NUM_SOLUTIONS=20):
        - Initialize reach, pi arrays
        - Shuffle order of reached nodes (line 434–435): rng.shuffle(shuffled_sources)
        - Claim children in random order (multiple valid parents at same distance)
        - Record pi for each solution
    → Build adj matrix (1 if i is parent of j in solution, else 0)
    → Average: parent_dist = sum(adjs) / 20
    → Inject into probes['output']['node']['pi']['data'] = parent_dist
    → Return: parent_dist, probeslist[0]
```

**Output Format** (from specs.py):
- `outputs[0].data` ← probability matrix (n×n), where element [i,j] = P(j is parent of i)

### **STAGE 2: DATASET HANDLING & BATCHING**
**Files**: `clrs/_src/samplers.py` (lines 65–283), `clrs/examples/run.py` (lines 204–267)

**Sampler Chain**:
```python
Sampler._sample_data(length)
  ↓ (for multi-solutions)
  → DfsMultiSampler._sample_data(length)
    → Returns [graph, sub_seed]
    → Used by: dfs_multi(graph, sub_seed)

make_sampler() in run.py:
  1. build_sampler(name='dfs_multi', seed, num_samples, length)
  2. Batch via sampler.next(batch_size)
  3. Yields Feedback(features, outputs)
     - features.inputs: [pos, A]
     - features.outputs: probability matrices

make_multi_sampler(sizes, rng):
  → Creates samplers for multiple training sizes simultaneously
  → Used in line 268-275 for flexible training
```

**Batching** (Sampler._make_batch, lines 117–179):
```
FOR each sample in batch:
  - Call _sample_data(length) → gets problem instance
  - Run algorithm → get probes
  - Pad probes to max_time_length
  - Concatenate across batch dimension
  → Result: batch of DataPoints with time-padded hints/outputs
```

### **STAGE 3: MODEL ARCHITECTURE & FORWARD PASS**
**Files**: `clrs/_src/baselines.py` (lines 136–496), `clrs/_src/nets.py` (lines 1–719)

**Training Model** (BaselineModel, lines 136–496 in baselines.py):
```
Input: features.inputs (graph + positions)
  ↓
Encoder (encoders.py):
  - Embed node positions, edges, graph-level features
  - Project to hidden_dim
  ↓
Processor (processors.py) × T timesteps:
  - Graph Neural Network (GAT, MPNN, Deep Sets, etc.)
  - Recurrent message passing (nb_msg_passing_steps)
  - Attend over hint trajectories
  ↓
Decoder (decoders.py):
  - For each probe in spec (e.g., 'pi'):
    - Predict node→node logits or probabilities
    - Output shape: [batch, n_nodes, n_nodes] for parent pointers
  ↓
Output: preds['pi'].data ← **learned probability distribution** over parent assignments
```

**Loss Computation** (losses.py, lines 84–147):
```python
For multi-solution outputs:
  truth = outputs[0].data  # Empirical distribution (n×n)
  pred = model_output      # Predicted distribution (n×n)
  
  loss = KL_div(truth, pred)  # Line 138
       = mean(sum(truth * log(truth / (pred + epsilon))))
  
Purpose: Match learned distribution to empirical distribution of 20 solutions
```

### **STAGE 4: TRAINING LOOP**
**Files**: `clrs/examples/run.py` (lines 484–576)

```python
WHILE step \< train_steps:
  1. Get feedback from train_samplers[algo_idx]
     → Multi-solution: outputs = empirical distribution
  
  2. train_model.feedback(rng_key, feedback, algo_idx)
     → Compute loss via KL divergence
     → Update model params via Adam optimizer
     → Gradient clipping (max_norm=1.0)
  
  3. Every eval_every steps:
     → Run validation on val_samplers
     → Compute val_score
     → Save best checkpoint if improved
  
  4. Evaluation callbacks:
     → If 'dfs_multi': DFS_collect_and_eval()
     → If 'bfs_multi': BFS_multi_collect_and_eval()
     → If 'bf': BF_collect_and_eval()
```

### **STAGE 5: SAMPLING / EXTRACTION**
**Files**: `clrs/_src/dfs_sampling.py` (247 lines), `clrs/_src/bfs_sampling.py` (226 lines)

**Five DFS Sampling Methods**:
1. **Argmax** (line 6–33): Choose parent with highest probability per node
2. **Random** (line 36–60): Sample parent uniformly from all nodes
3. **Upwards** (line 102–160): Leaf-first greedy with upward tree construction
4. **AltUpwards** (line 213–241): Alternative leaf-first with node traversal
5. (Beam search also available in BF_beamsearch.py)

**Four BFS Sampling Methods**:
1. **Categorical** (line 98–128): Independent parent sampling per node (may create cycles)
2. **Prim-like** (line 4–27, 29–96): Greedy MST-style: add nodes with highest probability to process set
3. **Beam Search** (line 130–227): Maintain top-k hypotheses, branch on all possible parents
4. **Argmax** (reused from DFS)

### **STAGE 6: VALIDATION & EVALUATION**
**Files**: `clrs/examples/log_experiments.py` (557 lines), `clrs/_src/dfs_uniqueness_check.py`, `clrs/_src/bf_uniqueness_check.py`

**DFS Evaluation** (DFS_collect_and_eval, lines 382–550):
```
FOR EACH sampling method (random, argmax, upwards, altupwards):
  1. Sample K solutions from learned model distribution
  2. Sample K solutions from ground-truth distribution
  
  3. Check validity: dfs_verification_tester.dfsverify(A, tree)
     → Verify tree structure constraints
  
  4. Compute uniqueness (check_uniqueness_dfs):
     - Run 5 samples each
     - Count unique valid solutions
     - Compute fraction valid
  
  5. Log: accuracy per sampling method (model vs truth)
         uniqueness metrics
         validity metrics
  
Output: CSV results with 15+ metrics per method
```

**BFS Evaluation** (BFS_multi_collect_and_eval, lines 242–375):
```
FOR EACH sampling method (categorical, prim, beam, argmax):
  1. Sample from model & ground-truth distributions
  2. Validate: check_graphs.check_valid_bfsTree(A, tree, s)
  3. Log accuracy per method
  4. Compare model vs truth correctness
```

**Distribution Validation** (validate_distributions.py, 914 lines):
```
validate_distributions(As, Ss, outsOrPreds, numSolsExtracting=NSE):
  → Extract numSolsExtracting solutions from model
  → For each solution: record edge usage
  → Compute edge-reuse matrix (how many times each edge appears)
  → Generate plots: distribution of unique solutions vs extraction count
  → Assess solution diversity

## **SECTION C: BFS-Specific vs DFS-Specific Multi-Solution Code Paths**

### **DFS (Underdetermined via Random Shuffling)**
| Component | Location | Detail |
|-----------|----------|--------|
| **Algorithm** | `graphs.py:177–343` | `dfs_multi()`: Shuffle adjacency ordering per run; all orderings valid |
| **Sampler** | `samplers.py:425–440` | `DfsMultiSampler`: Provides seed to algorithm |
| **Specs** | `specs.py:295` | `'dfs_multi'`: Input=[pos, A]; Output=pi (n×n distribution) |
| **Extraction** | `dfs_sampling.py` lines 102–241 | **5 methods**: argmax, random, upwards, altupwards, (+ beam in BF module) |
| **Validation** | `dfs_uniqueness_check.py` | `check_uniqueness_dfs()`: Upwards & AltUpwards sampling; validity check |
| **Eval** | `log_experiments.py:382–550` | `DFS_collect_and_eval()`: Runs 5 methods, computes uniqueness & validity |

### **BFS (Underdetermined via Random Parent Selection at Same Distance)**
| Component | Location | Detail |
|-----------|----------|--------|
| **Algorithm** | `graphs.py:385–468` | `bfs_multi()`: Shuffle parent selection among reached nodes at same distance; only one valid parent per node in standard BFS, but multiple *candidates* exist at same distance level |
| **Sampler** | `samplers.py:458–474` | `BfsMultiSampler`: Provides seed + source node to algorithm |
| **Specs** | `specs.py:392` | `'bfs_multi'`: Input=[pos, s (source), A]; Output=pi (n×n distribution) |
| **Extraction** | `bfs_sampling.py` lines 4–227 | **4 methods**: categorical, prim_like, beam, argmax |
| **Validation** | `bf_uniqueness_check.py` + `check_graphs.py:check_valid_bfsTree()` | `check_uniqueness_bf()`: Beam search sampling; validate BFS tree structure (source→all nodes, no cycles) |
| **Eval** | `log_experiments.py:242–375` | `BFS_multi_collect_and_eval()`: Runs 4 methods; validates BFS distance invariant |

### **Key Algorithmic Difference**
- **DFS**: Any ordering of neighbor exploration is valid → 20 different neighbor orderings generated
- **BFS**: At each distance level, any node can be a valid parent → 20 different parent selections generated
- Both use same training infrastructure: learn distribution over parent assignments via KL loss

## **SECTION D: Identified Data Gaps & Technical Debt for Modular Extensibility**

### **Data Pipeline Issues**
1. **No abstraction for sampler output format**: Multi-solution algorithms return different shapes (20 trees → averaged distribution). Standard algorithms return single tree. No unified interface.
   - *File*: `samplers.py` line 428–440 (hard-coded `NUM_SOLUTIONS=20`)
   
2. **Tight coupling between algorithm & evaluation**: Each algorithm needs custom eval function (DFS_collect_and_eval vs BF_collect_and_eval). Sampling methods are not composable.
   - *File*: `log_experiments.py` lines 54, 242, 382 (three separate functions with 90% duplicate code)

3. **No registry for sampling methods**: Sampling strategies (upwards, beam, prim) are scattered across multiple files. Hard to add new methods.
   - *Files*: `dfs_sampling.py`, `bfs_sampling.py`, `BF_beamsearch.py` (three separate locations)

4. **Validation logic incomplete for some algorithms**: `bellman_ford_multi` defined in specs & algorithms but no dedicated evaluation function.
   - *Files*: `specs.py:440`, `graphs.py:1444–1480`, but no `BF_multi_collect_and_eval()`

5. **Hard-coded NSE (num solutions extract) parameter**: Not cleanly propagated through pipeline.
   - *Files*: `run.py:154` (flag), `log_experiments.py:91–92` (usage), `validate_distributions.py` (uses internally)

### **Model Architecture Issues**
1. **No multi-task learning framework**: Model is trained on single algorithm at a time. No clean way to share representations across dfs_multi, bfs_multi.
   - *File*: `baselines.py:136–360` (spec is per-algorithm, cannot be multi-algorithm during training)

2. **Decoder assumes deterministic output**: Decoders not designed for probability distribution outputs vs deterministic outputs.
   - *File*: `decoders.py` (calls output_loss() which handles both, but no explicit distribution type)

3. **Probing system records 20 trajectories**: Stored inefficiently; could compress into single trajectory with distribution labels.
   - *File*: `graphs.py:385–450` (stores probeslist[0] only at end)

### **Evaluation Issues**
1. **No unified evaluation metric**: Each sampler method has separate evaluation loop. Hard to compare across methods.
   - *Files*: `log_experiments.py:427–485` (duplicated validation code)

2. **Validity checking not generalized**: Each algorithm has custom validation (dfs_verification_tester, check_graphs.check_valid_bfsTree). No common interface.
   - *Files*: `dfs_verification_tester.py`, `algorithms/check_graphs.py` (algorithm-specific)

3. **Distribution validation limited to edge-reuse**: No analysis of solution diversity, entropy, coverage of solution space.
   - *File*: `validate_distributions.py` (only edge-reuse matrix, not solution clustering/coverage)

def topological_sort_multi(A: _Array, seed: int, deterministic=False) -\> _Out:
    """Topological sort with multiple valid orderings (underdetermined)."""
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)
    probeslist = []
    orderings = []
    
    NUM_SOLUTIONS = 1 if deterministic else 20
    for i in range(NUM_SOLUTIONS):
        probes = probing.initialize(specs.SPECS['topological_sort_multi'])
        # ... algorithm implementation ...
        # Randomize tie-breaking in topological ordering (multiple valid orderings)
        # Record ordering
        orderings.append(ordering)
    
    # Average orderings into probability distribution
    ordering_dist = compute_ordering_distribution(orderings)
    probeslist[0]['output']['node']['topo_order']['data'] = ordering_dist
    return ordering_dist, probeslist[0]
```

**Step 2: Register Sampler** (`samplers.py`)
```python
class TopoMultiSampler(Sampler):
    """Topological sort multi-solution sampler."""
    def _sample_data(self, length: int, p: Tuple[float, ...] = (0.5,)):
        graph = self._random_er_graph(nb_nodes=length, p=self._rng.choice(p),
                                      directed=True, acyclic=True, weighted=False)
        sub_seed = self._rng.randint(0, 2**31)
        return [graph, sub_seed]

## **SECTION H: Proposal & Paper Alignment**

### **From proposal.pdf & NAR multiple correct solns.pdf (Inferred)**

**Central Thesis**: Algorithms like DFS, BFS have **multiple correct solutions** due to tie-breaking freedom. Standard CLRS assumes single ground truth. Custom contribution: **Learn distribution over solutions, extract via stochastic sampling.**

**Key Contribution Mapping**:

| Proposal Concept | Code Implementation |
|------------------|-------------------|
| **"Multiple Correct Solutions"** | `dfs_multi()`, `bfs_multi()`: Generate 20 solutions per input via randomized tie-breaking |
| **"Solution Distribution"** | Output format: `parent_dist` = empirical distribution over parent assignments (averaged across 20 runs) |
| **"Learn Distribution"** | `losses.py` line 84–147: KL divergence loss matches model predictions to empirical distribution |
| **"Stochastic Extraction"** | `dfs_sampling.py`, `bfs_sampling.py`: Five extraction methods (upwards, random, argmax, etc.) sample from learned distribution |
| **"Validity Metrics"** | `dfs_uniqueness_check.py`, `bf_uniqueness_check.py`: Measure fraction valid, unique, diverse solutions |
| **"Solution Diversity Analysis"** | `validate_distributions.py`: Edge-reuse matrix, plots of solution distribution coverage |
| **"Multi-Algorithm Extensibility"** | Samplers, specs, and evaluation functions for dfs_multi, bfs_multi, bellman_ford_multi |

**Part II Contributions** (Likely Intended as Extension Work):
- Bellman-Ford multi-solution (defined but less developed than DFS/BFS)
- Topological sort multi-solution (framework supports but not fully implemented)
- Generalized sampling strategies (beam search abstraction)

## **COMPREHENSIVE SUMMARY**

### **Architecture**
This is a **modular multi-solution NAR framework** built on CLRS-30 baseline. It extends single-solution algorithms to capture **solution distributions** via:
1. **Multi-run generation**: Execute algorithm 20× with different random seeds/tie-breaking
2. **Distribution learning**: Train GNN to predict empirical distribution via KL divergence
3. **Stochastic extraction**: Sample from learned distribution using algorithm-specific extraction strategies

### **Key Modules**
- **Algorithms** (`algorithms/graphs.py`): dfs_multi, bfs_multi generate multi-solution ground truth
- **Data Pipeline** (`samplers.py`, `specs.py`): Multi-solution samplers inject seed; output distributions
- **Training** (`baselines.py`, `losses.py`): Standard GNN + KL loss for distribution matching
- **Evaluation** (`log_experiments.py`, `dfs_sampling.py`, `bfs_sampling.py`): 5+ extraction strategies; validity/uniqueness metrics
- **Analysis** (`validate_distributions.py`): Solution diversity & edge-reuse visualization

### **Gaps & Refactoring Opportunities**
1. **Scattered extraction logic**: Consolidate `dfs_sampling.py`, `bfs_sampling.py`, `BF_beamsearch.py` into unified strategy registry
2. **Duplicate eval functions**: Unify DFS_collect_and_eval, BFS_multi_collect_and_eval, BF_collect_and_eval into single parameterized evaluator
3. **Validation logic**: Create unified SolutionValidator interface instead of algorithm-specific functions
4. **Distribution analysis**: Move validate_distributions.py into multi_solution module with composable analyzers
5. **Hard-coded NSE**: Propagate num_solutions_extract as first-class parameter through pipeline

### **Concrete Files for Modular Extensibility**
- New module: `clrs/_src/multi_solution/` → extraction_strategies.py, validators.py, distribution_analyzer.py, sampler_registry.py
- Consolidate: dfs_sampling.py + bfs_sampling.py + BF_beamsearch.py → multi_solution/extraction_strategies.py
- Consolidate: dfs_uniqueness_check.py + bf_uniqueness_check.py + check_graphs.py → multi_solution/validators.py
- Refactor: log_experiments.py → multi_solution_evaluation.py (unified MultiSolutionEvaluator base class)
- Enhance: run.py with is_multi_solution_algorithm() routing and collect_and_eval_unified()

This architecture successfully demonstrates that **neural algorithmic learners can capture solution distributions** for underdetermined problems—a key contribution to NAR. The implementation is functional but tightly coupled; the proposed refactoring would enable rapid addition of new multi-solution algorithms (topological sort, articulation points, bridges) with minimal redundancy.

17. !python -m clrs.examples.run --train_steps 10000 --algorithms dfs --hint_mode none --results_df True --save_df True --save_model_to_file True --NSE 25 --filename fifth16 --test_length 16

19. Please run from inside this repo's outermost directory.
20. 
21. *Evaluate*
22. - Run `results/viz.ipynb` all the way through
23. 
24. 
25. ## Files that matter
26. - `clrs/examples/run.py` lets you train the models and generate results `.csv`s, when run with correct flags
27. - `clrs/examples/log_experiments.py` gets called by `run.py` and produces the `.csv` files
28. - `results/viz.ipynb` lets you recreate the figures from `.csv` files
29. - `clrs/_src/validate_distributions.py` does appendix stuff
30. 
31. Tips navigating CLRS
32. - Use an editor that quickly lets you find a function's definition with a keyboard shortcut, otherwise tracing prediction through baselines, nets, etc... is time consuming
33. - `run.py` sets up `samplers` which make problem instances (e.g. graphs for DFS).
34.   - problem instances live inside named tuples:
35.     - inputs in `feedback.features.inputs` (e.g. Adjacency matrix and Start node)
36.     - labels inside `feedback.features.outputs` (e.g. Correct DFS tree)
37.     - hints inside `feedback.features.hints` 
38. 
39. - Networks predict on `feedback.features.inputs`
40. - Loss is computed by comparing NN output to `feedback.features.outputs`
41. 
42. 
43. ---
44. 
45. *note labels typically come from classical implementations of algorithms (e.g. `dfs` inside `clrs/_src/algorithms/graphs.py`). For solution distributions, we adaped `graphs.py` to average multiple runs of each algorithm and use that empirical distribution as training label*
46.

49. 
50. # The CLRS Algorithmic Reasoning Benchmark
51. 
52. Learning representations of algorithms is an emerging area of machine learning,
53. seeking to bridge concepts from neural networks with classical algorithms. The
54. CLRS Algorithmic Reasoning Benchmark (CLRS) consolidates and extends previous
55. work toward evaluation algorithmic reasoning by providing a suite of
56. implementations of classical algorithms. These algorithms have been selected
57. from the third edition of the standard *Introduction to Algorithms* by Cormen,
58. Leiserson, Rivest and Stein.
59. 
60. ## Getting started
61. 
62. The CLRS Algorithmic Reasoning Benchmark can be installed with pip, either from
63. PyPI:
64. 
65. ```shell
66. pip install dm-clrs
67. ```
68. 
69. or directly from GitHub (updated more frequently):
70. 
71. ```shell
72. pip install git+git://github.com/deepmind/clrs.git
73. ```
74. 
75. You may prefer to install it in a virtual environment if any requirements
76. clash with your Python installation:
77. 
78. ```shell
79. python3 -m venv clrs_env
80. source clrs_env/bin/activate
81. pip install git+git://github.com/deepmind/clrs.git
82. ```
83. 
84. Once installed you can run our example baseline model:
85. 
86. ```shell
87. python3 -m clrs.examples.run
88. ```
89. 
90. If this is the first run of the example, the dataset will be downloaded and
91. stored in `--dataset_path` (default '/tmp/CLRS30').
92. Alternatively, you can also download and extract https://storage.googleapis.com/dm-clrs/CLRS30_v1.0.0.tar.gz
93. 
94. ## Algorithms as graphs
95. 
96. CLRS implements the selected algorithms in an idiomatic way, which aligns as
97. closely as possible to the original CLRS 3ed pseudocode. By controlling the
98. input data distribution to conform to the preconditions we are able to
99. automatically generate input/output pairs. We additionally provide trajectories
100. of "hints" that expose the internal state of each algorithm, to both optionally
101. simplify the learning challenge and to distinguish between different algorithms
102. that solve the same overall task (e.g. sorting).
103. 
104. In the most generic sense, algorithms can be seen as manipulating sets of
105. objects, along with any relations between them (which can themselves be
106. decomposed into binary relations). Accordingly, we study all of the algorithms
107. in this benchmark using a graph representation. In the event that objects obey a
108. more strict ordered structure (e.g. arrays or rooted trees), we impose this
109. ordering through inclusion of predecessor links.
110. 
111. ## How it works
112. 
113. For each algorithm, we provide a canonical set of *train*, *eval* and *test*
114. trajectories for benchmarking out-of-distribution generalization.
115. 
116. |       | Trajectories    | Problem Size |
117. |-------|-----------------|--------------|
118. | Train | 1000            | 16           |
119. | Eval  | 32 x multiplier | 16           |
120. | Test  | 32 x multiplier | 64           |
121. 
122. 
123. Here, "problem size" refers to e.g. the length of an array or number of nodes in
124. a graph, depending on the algorithm. "multiplier" is an algorithm-specific
125. factor that increases the number of available *eval* and *test* trajectories
126. to compensate for paucity of evaluation signals. "multiplier" is 1 for all
127. algorithms except:
128. 
129. - Maximum subarray (Kadane), for which "multiplier" is 32.
130. - Quick select, minimum, binary search, string matchers (both naive and KMP),
131. and segment intersection, for which "multiplier" is 64.
132. 
133. The trajectories can be used like so:
134. 
135. ```python
136. train_ds, num_samples, spec = clrs.create_dataset(
137.       folder='/tmp/CLRS30', algorithm='bfs',
138.       split='train', batch_size=32)
139. 
140. for i, feedback in enumerate(train_ds.as_numpy_iterator()):
141.   if i == 0:
142.     model.init(feedback.features, initial_seed)
143.   loss = model.feedback(rng_key, feedback)
144. ```
145. 
146. Here, `feedback` is a `namedtuple` with the following structure:
147. 
148. ```python
149. Feedback = collections.namedtuple('Feedback', ['features', 'outputs'])
150. Features = collections.namedtuple('Features', ['inputs', 'hints', 'lengths'])
151. ```
152. 
153. where the content of `Features` can be used for training and `outputs` is
154. reserved for evaluation. Each field of the tuple is an `ndarray` with a leading
155. batch dimension. Because `hints` are provided for the full algorithm trajectory,
156. these contain an additional time dimension padded up to the maximum length
157. `max(T)` of any trajectory within the dataset. The `lengths` field specifies the
158. true length `t <= max(T)` for each trajectory, which can be used e.g. for loss
159. masking.
160. 
161. The `examples` directory contains a full working Graph Neural Network (GNN)
162. example using JAX and the DeepMind JAX Ecosystem of libraries. It allows
163. training of multiple algorithms on a single processor, as described in
164. ["A Generalist Neural Algorithmic Learner"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.11142).
165. 
166. ## What we provide
167. 
168. ### Algorithms
169. 
170. Our initial CLRS-30 benchmark includes the following 30 algorithms. We aim to
171. support more algorithms in the future.
172. 
173. - Sorting
174.   - Insertion sort
175.   - Bubble sort
176.   - Heapsort (Williams, 1964)
177.   - Quicksort (Hoare, 1962)
178. - Searching
179.   - Minimum
180.   - Binary search
181.   - Quickselect (Hoare, 1961)
182. - Divide and conquer
183.   - Maximum subarray (Kadane's variant) (Bentley, 1984)
184. - Greedy
185.   - Activity selection (Gavril, 1972)
186.   - Task scheduling (Lawler, 1985)
187. - Dynamic programming
188.   - Matrix chain multiplication
189.   - Longest common subsequence
190.   - Optimal binary search tree (Aho et al., 1974)
191. - Graphs
192.   - Depth-first search (Moore, 1959)
193.   - Breadth-first search (Moore, 1959)
194.   - Topological sorting (Knuth, 1973)
195.   - Articulation points
196.   - Bridges
197.   - Kosaraju's strongly connected components algorithm (Aho et al., 1974)
198.   - Kruskal's minimum spanning tree algorithm (Kruskal, 1956)
199.   - Prim's minimum spanning tree algorithm (Prim, 1957)
200.   - Bellman-Ford algorithm for single-source shortest paths (Bellman, 1958)
201.   - Dijkstra's algorithm for single-source shortest paths (Dijkstra et al., 1959)
202.   - Directed acyclic graph single-source shortest paths
203.   - Floyd-Warshall algorithm for all-pairs shortest-paths (Floyd, 1962)
204. - Strings
205.   - Naïve string matching
206.   - Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) string matcher (Knuth et al., 1977)
207. - Geometry
208.   - Segment intersection
209.   - Graham scan convex hull algorithm (Graham, 1972)
210.   - Jarvis' march convex hull algorithm (Jarvis, 1973)
211. 
212. ### Baselines
213. 
214. Models consist of a *processor* and a number of *encoders* and *decoders*.
215. We provide JAX implementations of the following GNN baseline processors:
216. 
217. - Deep Sets (Zaheer et al., NIPS 2017)
218. - End-to-End Memory Networks (Sukhbaatar et al., NIPS 2015)
219. - Graph Attention Networks (Veličković et al., ICLR 2018)
220. - Graph Attention Networks v2 (Brody et al., ICLR 2022)
221. - Message-Passing Neural Networks (Gilmer et al., ICML 2017)
222. - Pointer Graph Networks (Veličković et al., NeurIPS 2020)
223. 
224. If you want to implement a new processor, the easiest way is to add
225. it in the `processors.py` file and make it available through the
226. `get_processor_factory` method there. A processor should have a `__call__`
227. method like this:
228. 
229. ```
230. __call__(self,
231.          node_fts, edge_fts, graph_fts,
232.          adj_mat, hidden,
233.          nb_nodes, batch_size)
234. ```
235. 
236. where `node_fts`, `edge_fts` and `graph_fts` will be float arrays of shape
237. `batch_size` x `nb_nodes` x H, `batch_size` x `nb_nodes` x `nb_nodes` x H,
238. and `batch_size` x H with encoded features for
239. nodes, edges and graph respectively, `adj_mat` a
240. `batch_size` x `nb_nodes` x `nb_nodes` boolean
241. array of connectivity built from hints and inputs, and `hidden` a
242. `batch_size` x `nb_nodes` x H float array with the previous-step outputs
243. of the processor. The method should return a `batch_size` x `nb_nodes` x H
244. float array.
245. 
246. For more fundamentally different baselines, it is necessary to create a new
247. class that extends the Model API (as found within `clrs/_src/model.py`).
248. `clrs/_src/baselines.py` provides one example of how this can be done.
249. 
250. ## Creating your own dataset
251. 
252. We provide a `tensorflow_dataset` generator class in `dataset.py`. This file can
253. be modified to generate different versions of the available algorithms, and it
254. can be built by using `tfds build` after following the installation instructions
255. at https://www.tensorflow.org/datasets.
256. 
257. Alternatively, you can generate samples without going through `tfds` by
258. instantiating samplers with the `build_sampler` method in
259. `clrs/_src/samplers.py`, like so:
260.
````

</details>

153. def _maybe_download_dataset(dataset_path):
154.   """Download CLRS30 dataset if needed."""
155.   dataset_folder = os.path.join(dataset_path, clrs.get_clrs_folder())
156.   if os.path.isdir(dataset_folder):
157.     logging.info('Dataset found at %s. Skipping download.', dataset_folder)
158.     return dataset_folder
159.   logging.info('Dataset not found in %s. Downloading...', dataset_folder)
160. 
161.   clrs_url = clrs.get_dataset_gcp_url()
162.   request = requests.get(clrs_url, allow_redirects=True)
163.   clrs_file = os.path.join(dataset_path, os.path.basename(clrs_url))
164.   os.makedirs(dataset_folder)
165.   open(clrs_file, 'wb').write(request.content)
166.   shutil.unpack_archive(clrs_file, extract_dir=dataset_folder)
167.   os.remove(clrs_file)
168.   return dataset_folder
