136. class BaselineModel(model.Model):
137.   """Model implementation with selectable message passing algorithm."""
138. 
139.   def __init__(
140.       self,
141.       spec: Union[_Spec, List[_Spec]],
142.       dummy_trajectory: Union[List[_Feedback], _Feedback],
143.       processor_factory: processors.ProcessorFactory,
144.       hidden_dim: int = 32,
145.       encode_hints: bool = False,
146.       decode_hints: bool = True,
147.       encoder_init: str = 'default',
148.       use_lstm: bool = False,
149.       learning_rate: float = 0.005,
150.       grad_clip_max_norm: float = 0.0,
151.       checkpoint_path: str = '/tmp/clrs3',
152.       freeze_processor: bool = False,
153.       dropout_prob: float = 0.0,
154.       hint_teacher_forcing: float = 0.0,
155.       hint_repred_mode: str = 'soft',
156.       name: str = 'base_model',
157.       nb_msg_passing_steps: int = 1,
158.   ):
159.     """Constructor for BaselineModel.
160. 
161.     The model consists of encoders, processor and decoders. It can train
162.     and evaluate either a single algorithm or a set of algorithms; in the
163.     latter case, a single processor is shared among all the algorithms, while
164.     the encoders and decoders are separate for each algorithm.
165. 
166.     Args:
167.       spec: Either a single spec for one algorithm, or a list of specs for
168.         multiple algorithms to be trained and evaluated.
169.       dummy_trajectory: Either a single feedback batch, in the single-algorithm
170.         case, or a list of feedback batches, in the multi-algorithm case, that
171.         comply with the `spec` (or list of specs), to initialize network size.
172.       processor_factory: A callable that takes an `out_size` parameter
173.         and returns a processor (see `processors.py`).
174.       hidden_dim: Size of the hidden state of the model, i.e., size of the
175.         message-passing vectors.
176.       encode_hints: Whether to provide hints as model inputs.
177.       decode_hints: Whether to provide hints as model outputs.
178.       encoder_init: The initialiser type to use for the encoders.
179.       use_lstm: Whether to insert an LSTM after message passing.
180.       learning_rate: Learning rate for training.
181.       grad_clip_max_norm: if greater than 0, the maximum norm of the gradients.
182.       checkpoint_path: Path for loading/saving checkpoints.
183.       freeze_processor: If True, the processor weights will be frozen and
184.         only encoders and decoders (and, if used, the lstm) will be trained.
185.       dropout_prob: Dropout rate in the message-passing stage.
186.       hint_teacher_forcing: Probability of using ground-truth hints instead
187.         of predicted hints as inputs during training (only relevant if
188.         `encode_hints`=True)
189.       hint_repred_mode: How to process predicted hints when fed back as inputs.
190.         Only meaningful when `encode_hints` and `decode_hints` are True.
191.         Options are:
192.           - 'soft', where we use softmaxes for categoricals, pointers
193.               and mask_one, and sigmoids for masks. This will allow gradients
194.               to flow through hints during training.
195.           - 'hard', where we use argmax instead of softmax, and hard
196.               thresholding of masks. No gradients will go through the hints
197.               during training; even for scalar hints, which don't have any
198.               kind of post-processing, gradients will be stopped.
199.           - 'hard_on_eval', which is soft for training and hard for evaluation.
200.       name: Model name.
201.       nb_msg_passing_steps: Number of message passing steps per hint.
202. 
203.     Raises:
204.       ValueError: if `encode_hints=True` and `decode_hints=False`.
205.     """
206.     super(BaselineModel, self).__init__(spec=spec)
207. 
208.     if encode_hints and not decode_hints:
209.       raise ValueError('`encode_hints=True`, `decode_hints=False` is invalid.')
210. 
211.     assert hint_repred_mode in ['soft', 'hard', 'hard_on_eval']
212. 
213.     self.decode_hints = decode_hints
214.     self.checkpoint_path = checkpoint_path
215.     self.name = name
216.     self._freeze_processor = freeze_processor
217.     if grad_clip_max_norm != 0.0:
218.       optax_chain = [optax.clip_by_global_norm(grad_clip_max_norm),
219.                      optax.scale_by_adam(),
220.                      optax.scale(-learning_rate)]
221.       self.opt = optax.chain(*optax_chain)
222.     else:
223.       self.opt = optax.adam(learning_rate)
224. 
225.     self.nb_msg_passing_steps = nb_msg_passing_steps
226. 
227.     self.nb_dims = []
228.     if isinstance(dummy_trajectory, _Feedback):
229.       assert len(self._spec) == 1
230.       dummy_trajectory = [dummy_trajectory]
231.     for traj in dummy_trajectory:
232.       nb_dims = {}
233.       for inp in traj.features.inputs:
234.         nb_dims[inp.name] = inp.data.shape[-1]
235.       for hint in traj.features.hints:
236.         nb_dims[hint.name] = hint.data.shape[-1]
237.       for outp in traj.outputs:
238.         nb_dims[outp.name] = outp.data.shape[-1]
239.       self.nb_dims.append(nb_dims)
240. 
241.     self._create_net_fns(hidden_dim, encode_hints, processor_factory, use_lstm,
242.                          encoder_init, dropout_prob, hint_teacher_forcing,
243.                          hint_repred_mode)
244.     self._device_params = None
245.     self._device_opt_state = None
246.     self.opt_state_skeleton = None
247. 
248.   def _create_net_fns(self, hidden_dim, encode_hints, processor_factory,
249.                       use_lstm, encoder_init, dropout_prob,
250.                       hint_teacher_forcing, hint_repred_mode):
251.     def _use_net(*args, **kwargs):
252.       return nets.Net(self._spec, hidden_dim, encode_hints, self.decode_hints,
253.                       processor_factory, use_lstm, encoder_init,
254.                       dropout_prob, hint_teacher_forcing,
255.                       hint_repred_mode,
256.                       self.nb_dims, self.nb_msg_passing_steps)(*args, **kwargs)
257. 
258.     self.net_fn = hk.transform(_use_net)
259.     pmap_args = dict(axis_name='batch', devices=jax.local_devices())
260.     n_devices = jax.local_device_count()
261.     func, static_arg, extra_args = (
262.         (jax.jit, 'static_argnums', {}) if n_devices == 1 else
263.         (jax.pmap, 'static_broadcasted_argnums', pmap_args))
264.     pmean = functools.partial(jax.lax.pmean, axis_name='batch')
265.     self._maybe_pmean = pmean if n_devices > 1 else lambda x: x
266.     extra_args[static_arg] = 3
267.     self.jitted_grad = func(self._compute_grad, **extra_args)
268.     extra_args[static_arg] = 4
269.     self.jitted_feedback = func(self._feedback, donate_argnums=[0, 3],
270.                                 **extra_args)
271.     extra_args[static_arg] = [3, 4, 5]
272.     self.jitted_predict = func(self._predict, **extra_args)
273.     extra_args[static_arg] = [3, 4]
274.     self.jitted_accum_opt_update = func(accum_opt_update, donate_argnums=[0, 2],
275.                                         **extra_args)
276. 
277.   def init(self, features: Union[_Features, List[_Features]], seed: _Seed):
278.     if not isinstance(features, list):
279.       assert len(self._spec) == 1
280.       features = [features]
281.     self.params = self.net_fn.init(jax.random.PRNGKey(seed), features, True,  # pytype: disable=wrong-arg-types  # jax-ndarray
282.                                    algorithm_index=-1,
283.                                    return_hints=False,
284.                                    return_all_outputs=False)
285.     self.opt_state = self.opt.init(self.params)
286.     # We will use the optimizer state skeleton for traversal when we
287.     # want to avoid updating the state of params of untrained algorithms.
288.     self.opt_state_skeleton = self.opt.init(jnp.zeros(1))

292.     if self._device_params is None:

310.   def _compute_grad(self, params, rng_key, feedback, algorithm_index):
311.     lss, grads = jax.value_and_grad(self._loss)(
312.         params, rng_key, feedback, algorithm_index)
313.     return self._maybe_pmean(lss), self._maybe_pmean(grads)

315.   def _feedback(self, params, rng_key, feedback, opt_state, algorithm_index):
316.     lss, grads = jax.value_and_grad(self._loss)(
317.         params, rng_key, feedback, algorithm_index)
318.     grads = self._maybe_pmean(grads)
319.     params, opt_state = self._update_params(params, grads, opt_state,
320.                                             algorithm_index)
321.     lss = self._maybe_pmean(lss)
322.     return lss, params, opt_state

324.   def _predict(self, params, rng_key: hk.PRNGSequence, features: _Features,
325.                algorithm_index: int, return_hints: bool,
326.                return_all_outputs: bool):
327.     outs, hint_preds = self.net_fn.apply(
328.         params, rng_key, [features],
329.         repred=True, algorithm_index=algorithm_index,
330.         return_hints=return_hints,
331.         return_all_outputs=return_all_outputs)
332.     #print(outs) # EDITED
333.     outs = decoders.postprocess(self._spec[algorithm_index],
334.                                 outs,
335.                                 sinkhorn_temperature=0.1,
336.                                 sinkhorn_steps=50,
337.                                 hard=True,
338.                                 )
339.     return outs, hint_preds

399.         params, rng_key, [feedback.features],

422.             preds=[x[truth.name] for x in hint_preds],
423.             lengths=lengths,

425.         )

579.         repred=False,
580.         init_mp_state=False,
581.         algorithm_index=algorithm_index)
582. 
583.     nb_nodes = _nb_nodes(feedback, is_chunked=True)
584. 
585.     total_loss = 0.0
586.     is_first = feedback.features.is_first
587.     is_last = feedback.features.is_last
588. 
589.     # Calculate output loss.
590.     for truth in feedback.outputs:
591.       total_loss += losses.output_loss_chunked(
592.           truth=truth,
593.           pred=output_preds[truth.name],
594.           is_last=is_last,
595.           nb_nodes=nb_nodes,
596.       )
597. 
598.     # Optionally accumulate hint losses.
599.     if self.decode_hints:
600.       for truth in feedback.features.hints:
601.         loss = losses.hint_loss_chunked(
602.             truth=truth,
603.             pred=hint_preds[truth.name],
604.             is_first=is_first,
605.             nb_nodes=nb_nodes,
606.         )
607.         total_loss += loss
608. 
609.     return total_loss, (mp_state,)

611.   def _compute_grad(self, params, rng_key, feedback, mp_state, algorithm_index):
612.     (lss, (mp_state,)), grads = jax.value_and_grad(self._loss, has_aux=True)(
613.         params, rng_key, feedback, mp_state, algorithm_index)
614.     return self._maybe_pmean(lss), mp_state, self._maybe_pmean(grads)

617.                 algorithm_index):
618.     (lss, (mp_state,)), grads = jax.value_and_grad(self._loss, has_aux=True)(
619.         params, rng_key, feedback, mp_state, algorithm_index)
620.     grads = self._maybe_pmean(grads)
621.     params, opt_state = self._update_params(params, grads, opt_state,
622.                                             algorithm_index)
623.     lss = self._maybe_pmean(lss)
624.     return lss, params, opt_state, mp_state

626.   def compute_grad(
627.       self,
628.       rng_key: hk.PRNGSequence,
629.       feedback: _Feedback,
630.       algorithm_index: Optional[Tuple[int, int]] = None,
631.   ) -> Tuple[float, _Array]:
632.     """Compute gradients."""

634.     if algorithm_index is None:
635.       assert len(self._spec) == 1
636.       algorithm_index = (0, 0)
637.     length_index, algorithm_index = algorithm_index
638.     # Reusing init_mp_state improves performance.
639.     # The next, commented out line, should be used for proper state keeping.
640.     # mp_state = self.mp_states[length_index][algorithm_index]

649.     grads = _maybe_pick_first_pmapped(grads)
650.     mp_state = _maybe_restack_from_pmap(mp_state)

704. def _is_not_done_broadcast(lengths, i, tensor):
705.   is_not_done = (lengths > i + 1) * 1.0
706.   while len(is_not_done.shape) < len(tensor.shape):
707.     is_not_done = jnp.expand_dims(is_not_done, -1)

711. def accum_opt_update(params, grads, opt_state, opt, freeze_processor):
712.   """Update params from gradients collected from several algorithms."""
713.   # Average the gradients over all algos
714.   grads = jax.tree_util.tree_map(
715.       lambda *x: sum(x) / (sum([jnp.any(k) for k in x]) + 1e-12), *grads)
716.   updates, opt_state = opt.update(grads, opt_state)
717.   if freeze_processor:
718.     params_subset = _filter_out_processor(params)
719.     assert len(params) > len(params_subset)
720.     assert params_subset
721.     updates_subset = _filter_out_processor(updates)
722.     new_params = optax.apply_updates(params_subset, updates_subset)
723.     new_params = hk.data_structures.merge(params, new_params)
724.   else:
725.     new_params = optax.apply_updates(params, updates)
726. 
727.   return new_params, opt_state

731. def opt_update(opt, flat_grads, flat_opt_state):
732.   return opt.update(flat_grads, flat_opt_state)

735. def filter_null_grads(grads, opt, opt_state, opt_state_skeleton, algo_idx):
736.   """Compute updates ignoring params that have no gradients.
737. 
738.   This prevents untrained params (e.g., encoders/decoders for algorithms
739.   that are not being trained) to accumulate, e.g., momentum from spurious
740.   zero gradients.
741. 
742.   Note: this works as intended for "per-parameter" optimizer state, such as
743.     momentum. However, when the optimizer has some global state (such as the
744.     step counts in Adam), the global state will be updated every time,
745.     affecting also future updates of parameters that had null gradients in the
746.     current step.
747. 
748.   Args:
749.     grads: Gradients for all parameters.
750.     opt: Optax optimizer.
751.     opt_state: Optimizer state.
752.     opt_state_skeleton: A "skeleton" of optimizer state that has been
753.       initialized with scalar parameters. This serves to traverse each parameter
754.       of the otpimizer state during the opt state update.
755.     algo_idx: Index of algorithm, to filter out unused encoders/decoders.
756.       If None, no filtering happens.
757.   Returns:
758.     Updates and new optimizer state, where the parameters with null gradient
759.       have not been taken into account.
760.   """
761.   def _keep_in_algo(k, v):
762.     """Ignore params of encoders/decoders irrelevant for this algo."""
763.     # Note: in shared pointer decoder modes, we should exclude shared params
764.     #       for algos that do not have pointer outputs.
765.     if ((processors.PROCESSOR_TAG in k) or
766.         (f'algo_{algo_idx}_' in k)):
767.       return v
768.     return jax.tree_util.tree_map(lambda x: None, v)
769. 
770.   if algo_idx is None:
771.     masked_grads = grads
772.   else:
773.     masked_grads = {k: _keep_in_algo(k, v) for k, v in grads.items()}
774.   flat_grads, treedef = jax.tree_util.tree_flatten(masked_grads)
775.   flat_opt_state = jax.tree_util.tree_map(
776.       lambda _, x: x  # pylint:disable=g-long-lambda
777.       if isinstance(x, (np.ndarray, jax.Array))
778.       else treedef.flatten_up_to(x),
779.       opt_state_skeleton,
780.       opt_state,
781.   )
782. 
783.   # Compute updates only for the params with gradient.
784.   flat_updates, flat_opt_state = opt_update(opt, flat_grads, flat_opt_state)
785. 
786.   def unflatten(flat, original):
787.     """Restore tree structure, filling missing (None) leaves with original."""
788.     if isinstance(flat, (np.ndarray, jax.Array)):
789.       return flat
790.     return jax.tree_util.tree_map(lambda x, y: x if y is None else y, original,
791.                                   treedef.unflatten(flat))
792. 
793.   # Restore the state and updates tree structure.
794.   new_opt_state = jax.tree_util.tree_map(lambda _, x, y: unflatten(x, y),
795.                                          opt_state_skeleton, flat_opt_state,
796.                                          opt_state)
797.   updates = unflatten(flat_updates,
798.                       jax.tree_util.tree_map(lambda x: 0., grads))
799.   return updates, new_opt_state
800.

30. def fuse_perm_and_mask(perm: probing.DataPoint,
31.                        mask: probing.DataPoint) -> probing.DataPoint:
32.   """Replace permutation pointers active in the mask with self-pointers.
33. 
34.   Args:
35.     perm: a node permutation_pointer; data shape is expected to be
36.       [..., N, N], and ideally one-hot over the last two dimensions, although
37.       this method does not check for one-hotness.
38.     mask: a mask_one over nodes; data shape is expected to be
39.       [..., N], and ideally one-hot over the last dimension, although
40.       this method does not check for one-hotness.
41.   Returns:
42.     A node pointer with shape [..., N].
43.   """
44.   assert perm.type_ == specs.Type.PERMUTATION_POINTER
45.   assert perm.location == specs.Location.NODE
46.   assert mask.name == perm.name + '_mask'
47.   assert mask.type_ == specs.Type.MASK_ONE
48.   assert mask.location == specs.Location.NODE
49.   assert perm.data.shape[-1] == perm.data.shape[-2]
50.   assert perm.data.shape[:-1] == mask.data.shape
51.   data = np.where(mask.data > 0.5,
52.                   np.arange(perm.data.shape[-1]),  # self-pointers
53.                   np.argmax(perm.data, axis=-1))   # original pointers
54.   return probing.DataPoint(name=perm.name,
55.                            type_=specs.Type.POINTER,
56.                            location=perm.location,
57.                            data=data)
58. 
59. 
60. def _reduce_permutations_tuple(
61.     targets: Tuple[probing.DataPoint, ...]) -> Tuple[probing.DataPoint, ...]:
62.   """Reduce node pointer + mask_one permutation to just node pointer."""
63.   out_targets = []
64.   n_perms = 0
65.   i = 0
66.   while i < len(targets):
67.     truth = targets[i]
68.     #hi
69.     #print('in evalutation, truth=', truth)
70.     #print(truth.data)
71.     if truth.type_ != specs.Type.PERMUTATION_POINTER:
72.       out_targets.append(truth)
73.       i += 1
74.       continue
75.     truth_mask = targets[i + 1]
76.     out_targets.append(fuse_perm_and_mask(truth, truth_mask))
77.     i += 2
78.     n_perms += 1
79. 
80.   assert len(out_targets) == len(targets) - n_perms
81.   return tuple(out_targets)
82. 
83. 
84. def _reduce_permutations_dict(predictions: Result) -> Result:
85.   """Reduce node pointer + mask_one permutation to just node pointer."""
86.   out_preds = {}
87.   n_perms = 0
88.   for k, pred in predictions.items():
89.     if (k.endswith('_mask') and k[:-5] in predictions and
90.         predictions[k[:-5]].type_ == specs.Type.PERMUTATION_POINTER):
91.       # This mask will be processed with its associated permutation datapoint
92.       continue
93.     if pred.type_ != specs.Type.PERMUTATION_POINTER:
94.       out_preds[k] = pred
95.       continue
96.     pred_mask = predictions[k + '_mask']
97.     out_preds[k] = fuse_perm_and_mask(pred, pred_mask)
98.     n_perms += 1
99. 
100.   assert len(out_preds) == len(predictions) - n_perms
101.   return out_preds
102. 
103. 
104. def evaluate_hints(
105.     hints: Tuple[probing.DataPoint, ...],
106.     lengths: _Array,
107.     hint_preds: List[Result],
108. ) -> Dict[str, _Array]:
109.   """Evaluate hint predictions."""
110.   evals = {}
111.   hints = _reduce_permutations_tuple(hints)
112.   hint_preds = [_reduce_permutations_dict(h) for h in hint_preds]
113.   for truth in hints:
114.     assert truth.name in hint_preds[0]
115.     eval_along_time = [_evaluate(truth, p[truth.name],
116.                                  idx=i+1, lengths=lengths)
117.                        for (i, p) in enumerate(hint_preds)]
118.     evals[truth.name] = np.sum(
119.         [x * np.sum(i+1 < lengths)
120.          for i, x in enumerate(eval_along_time)]) / np.sum(lengths - 1)
121.     evals[truth.name + '_along_time'] = np.array(eval_along_time)
122. 
123.   # Unlike outputs, the hints sometimes include scalars, which don't have
124.   # a meaningful eval score. So we don't compute a global 'hint score' as we
125.   # do for outputs.
126.   return evals
127. 
128. 
129. def evaluate(
130.     outputs: Tuple[probing.DataPoint, ...],
131.     predictions: Result,
132. ) -> Dict[str, float]:
133.   """Evaluate output predictions."""
134.   evals = {}
135.   #print('in evaluate method, outputs=', outputs)
136.   outputs = _reduce_permutations_tuple(outputs)
137.   #print('in evaluate method, predictions=', predictions)
138.   #print(predictions[0].data)
139.   predictions = _reduce_permutations_dict(predictions)
140.   for truth in outputs:
141.     assert truth.name in predictions
142.     pred = predictions[truth.name]
143.     evals[truth.name] = _evaluate(truth, pred)
144.     #breakpoint()
145.   # Return a single scalar score that is the mean of all output scores.
146.   evals['score'] = sum([v.item() for v in evals.values()]) / len(evals)
147.   return evals
148. 
149. 
150. def _evaluate(truth, pred, idx=None, lengths=None):
151.   """Evaluate single prediction of hint or output."""
152.   #breakpoint()
153.   assert pred.name == truth.name
154.   assert pred.location == truth.location
155.   assert pred.type_ == truth.type_
156. 
157.   if truth.type_ not in _EVAL_FN:
158.     raise ValueError('Invalid type')
159.   truth_data = truth.data
160.   pred_data = pred.data
161.   if idx is not None:
162.     if np.all(idx >= lengths):
163.       return 0.
164.     truth_data = truth_data[idx][idx < lengths]
165.     #print('truth_data: {}', truth_data)
166.     pred_data = pred_data[idx < lengths]
167.   #print('getting here?')
168.   #breakpoint()
169.   return _EVAL_FN[truth.type_](pred_data, truth_data)
170. 
171. 
172. def _eval_one(pred, truth):
173.   mask = np.all(truth != specs.OutputClass.MASKED, axis=-1)
174.   return np.sum(
175.       (np.argmax(pred, -1) == np.argmax(truth, -1)) * mask) / np.sum(mask)
176. 
177. 
178. def _mask_fn(pred, truth):
179.   """Evaluate outputs of type MASK, and account for any class imbalance."""
180.   mask = (truth != specs.OutputClass.MASKED).astype(np.float32)
181. 
182.   # Use F1 score for the masked outputs to address any imbalance
183.   tp = np.sum((((pred > 0.5) * (truth > 0.5)) * 1.0) * mask)
184.   fp = np.sum((((pred > 0.5) * (truth < 0.5)) * 1.0) * mask)
185.   fn = np.sum((((pred < 0.5) * (truth > 0.5)) * 1.0) * mask)
186. 
187.   # Protect against division by zero
188.   if tp + fp > 0:
189.     precision = tp / (tp + fp)
190.   else:
191.     precision = np.float32(1.0)
192.   if tp + fn > 0:
193.     recall = tp / (tp + fn)
194.   else:
195.     recall = np.float32(1.0)
196. 
197.   if precision + recall > 0.0:
198.     f_1 = 2.0 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)
199.   else:
200.     f_1 = np.float32(0.0)
201. 
202.   return f_1
203. 
204. _EVAL_FN = {
205.     specs.Type.SCALAR:
206.         lambda pred, truth: np.mean((pred - truth)**2),
207.     specs.Type.MASK: _mask_fn,
208.     specs.Type.MASK_ONE:
209.         _eval_one,
210.     specs.Type.CATEGORICAL:
211.         _eval_one,
212.     specs.Type.POINTER:
213.         lambda pred, truth: np.mean((pred == truth) * 1.0),
214.     specs.Type.MULT_SOL:
215.         #FIXME eval scores best model based on highest score. We compute loss.
216.         #lambda pred, truth: np.mean(jax.scipy.special.kl_div(truth, pred)) FIXME! KL div has high values
217.         #lambda pred, truth: np.sum(truth * np.log((pred + 1e-8)/(truth + 1e-8))) # when truth is 0, inflates too much.
218.         #lambda pred, truth: -np.sum(truth * np.log(truth/pred+1e-8)) # pred 2less likely to be 0? more stable?
219.         #lambda pred, truth: np.sum(truth * (np.log(truth) - log(pred)))
220.         #lambda pred, truth: np.mean(np.abs(pred - truth) * 1.0), #_eval_one ##FIXME! Change to KLDIV
221.         #### Try proximity? maximizing 1-np.abs(pred-truth)
222.         lambda pred, truth: np.mean(1-np.abs(pred-truth)) # 1 - error. Report mean: typically, off by what
223. }
224.

74.   def __init__(
75.       self,
76.       spec: List[_Spec],

86.       nb_dims=None,
87.       nb_msg_passing_steps=1,
88.       name: str = 'net',
89.   ):
90.     """Constructs a `Net`."""
91.     super().__init__(name=name)
92. 
93.     self._dropout_prob = dropout_prob
94.     self._hint_teacher_forcing = hint_teacher_forcing
95.     self._hint_repred_mode = hint_repred_mode

106.   def _msg_passing_step(self,
107.                         mp_state: _MessagePassingScanState,
108.                         i: int,
109.                         hints: List[_DataPoint],

112.                         batch_size: int,

118.                         decs: Dict[str, Tuple[hk.Module]],
119.                         return_hints: bool,
120.                         return_all_outputs: bool
121.                         ):
122.     if self.decode_hints and not first_step:
123.       assert self._hint_repred_mode in ['soft', 'hard', 'hard_on_eval']
124.       hard_postprocess = (self._hint_repred_mode == 'hard' or
125.                           (self._hint_repred_mode == 'hard_on_eval' and repred))
126.       decoded_hint = decoders.postprocess(spec,
127.                                           mp_state.hint_preds,
128.                                           sinkhorn_temperature=0.1,
129.                                           sinkhorn_steps=25,
130.                                           hard=hard_postprocess)
131.     if repred and self.decode_hints and not first_step:
132.       cur_hint = []
133.       for hint in decoded_hint:
134.         cur_hint.append(decoded_hint[hint])
135.     else:
136.       cur_hint = []
137.       needs_noise = (self.decode_hints and not first_step and
138.                      self._hint_teacher_forcing < 1.0)
139.       if needs_noise:
140.         # For noisy teacher forcing, choose which examples in the batch to force
141.         force_mask = jax.random.bernoulli(
142.             hk.next_rng_key(), self._hint_teacher_forcing,
143.             (batch_size,))
144.       else:
145.         force_mask = None
146.       for hint in hints:
147.         hint_data = jnp.asarray(hint.data)[i]
148.         _, loc, typ = spec[hint.name]
149.         if needs_noise:
150.           if (typ == _Type.POINTER and
151.               decoded_hint[hint.name].type_ == _Type.SOFT_POINTER):
152.             # When using soft pointers, the decoded hints cannot be summarised
153.             # as indices (as would happen in hard postprocessing), so we need
154.             # to raise the ground-truth hint (potentially used for teacher
155.             # forcing) to its one-hot version.
156.             hint_data = hk.one_hot(hint_data, nb_nodes)
157.             typ = _Type.SOFT_POINTER
158.           hint_data = jnp.where(_expand_to(force_mask, hint_data),
159.                                 hint_data,
160.                                 decoded_hint[hint.name].data)
161.         cur_hint.append(
162.             probing.DataPoint(
163.                 name=hint.name, location=loc, type_=typ, data=hint_data))
164. 
165.     hiddens, output_preds_cand, hint_preds, lstm_state = self._one_step_pred(
166.         inputs, cur_hint, mp_state.hiddens,
167.         batch_size, nb_nodes, mp_state.lstm_state,
168.         spec, encs, decs, repred)
169. 
170.     if first_step:
171.       output_preds = output_preds_cand
172.     else:
173.       output_preds = {}
174.       for outp in mp_state.output_preds:
175.         is_not_done = _is_not_done_broadcast(lengths, i,
176.                                              output_preds_cand[outp])
177.         output_preds[outp] = is_not_done * output_preds_cand[outp] + (
178.             1.0 - is_not_done) * mp_state.output_preds[outp]
179. 
180.     new_mp_state = _MessagePassingScanState(  # pytype: disable=wrong-arg-types  # numpy-scalars
181.         hint_preds=hint_preds,
182.         output_preds=output_preds,
183.         hiddens=hiddens,
184.         lstm_state=lstm_state)
185.     # Save memory by not stacking unnecessary fields
186.     accum_mp_state = _MessagePassingScanState(  # pytype: disable=wrong-arg-types  # numpy-scalars
187.         hint_preds=hint_preds if return_hints else None,
188.         output_preds=output_preds if return_all_outputs else None,
189.         hiddens=None, lstm_state=None)
190. 
191.     # Complying to jax.scan, the first returned value is the state we carry over
192.     # the second value is the output that will be stacked over steps.
193.     return new_mp_state, accum_mp_state

195.   def __call__(self, features_list: List[_Features], repred: bool,
196.                algorithm_index: int,
197.                return_hints: bool,
198.                return_all_outputs: bool):
199.     """Process one batch of data.
200. 
201.     Args:
202.       features_list: A list of _Features objects, each with the inputs, hints
203.         and lengths for a batch o data corresponding to one algorithm.
204.         The list should have either length 1, at train/evaluation time,
205.         or length equal to the number of algorithms this Net is meant to
206.         process, at initialization.
207.       repred: False during training, when we have access to ground-truth hints.
208.         True in validation/test mode, when we have to use our own
209.         hint predictions.
210.       algorithm_index: Which algorithm is being processed. It can be -1 at
211.         initialisation (either because we are initialising the parameters of
212.         the module or because we are intialising the message-passing state),
213.         meaning that all algorithms should be processed, in which case
214.         `features_list` should have length equal to the number of specs of
215.         the Net. Otherwise, `algorithm_index` should be
216.         between 0 and `length(self.spec) - 1`, meaning only one of the
217.         algorithms will be processed, and `features_list` should have length 1.
218.       return_hints: Whether to accumulate and return the predicted hints,
219.         when they are decoded.
220.       return_all_outputs: Whether to return the full sequence of outputs, or
221.         just the last step's output.
222. 
223.     Returns:
224.       A 2-tuple with (output predictions, hint predictions)
225.       for the selected algorithm.
226.     """
227.     if algorithm_index == -1:
228.       algorithm_indices = range(len(features_list))
229.     else:
230.       algorithm_indices = [algorithm_index]
231.     assert len(algorithm_indices) == len(features_list)
232. 
233.     self.encoders, self.decoders = self._construct_encoders_decoders()
234.     self.processor = self.processor_factory(self.hidden_dim)
235. 
236.     # Optionally construct LSTM.
237.     if self.use_lstm:
238.       self.lstm = hk.LSTM(
239.           hidden_size=self.hidden_dim,
240.           name='processor_lstm')
241.       lstm_init = self.lstm.initial_state
242.     else:
243.       self.lstm = None
244.       lstm_init = lambda x: 0
245. 
246.     for algorithm_index, features in zip(algorithm_indices, features_list):
247.       inputs = features.inputs
248.       hints = features.hints
249.       lengths = features.lengths
250. 
251.       batch_size, nb_nodes = _data_dimensions(features)
252. 
253.       nb_mp_steps = max(1, hints[0].data.shape[0] - 1)
254.       hiddens = jnp.zeros((batch_size, nb_nodes, self.hidden_dim))
255. 
256.       if self.use_lstm:
257.         lstm_state = lstm_init(batch_size * nb_nodes)
258.         lstm_state = jax.tree_util.tree_map(
259.             lambda x, b=batch_size, n=nb_nodes: jnp.reshape(x, [b, n, -1]),
260.             lstm_state)
261.       else:
262.         lstm_state = None
263. 
264.       mp_state = _MessagePassingScanState(  # pytype: disable=wrong-arg-types  # numpy-scalars
265.           hint_preds=None, output_preds=None,
266.           hiddens=hiddens, lstm_state=lstm_state)
267. 
268.       # Do the first step outside of the scan because it has a different
269.       # computation graph.
270.       common_args = dict(
271.           hints=hints,
272.           repred=repred,
273.           inputs=inputs,
274.           batch_size=batch_size,
275.           nb_nodes=nb_nodes,
276.           lengths=lengths,
277.           spec=self.spec[algorithm_index],
278.           encs=self.encoders[algorithm_index],
279.           decs=self.decoders[algorithm_index],
280.           return_hints=return_hints,
281.           return_all_outputs=return_all_outputs,
282.           )
283.       mp_state, lean_mp_state = self._msg_passing_step(
284.           mp_state,
285.           i=0,
286.           first_step=True,
287.           **common_args)
288. 
289.       # Then scan through the rest.
290.       scan_fn = functools.partial(
291.           self._msg_passing_step,
292.           first_step=False,
293.           **common_args)
294. 
295.       output_mp_state, accum_mp_state = hk.scan(
296.           scan_fn,
297.           mp_state,
298.           jnp.arange(nb_mp_steps - 1) + 1,
299.           length=nb_mp_steps - 1)
300. 
301.     # We only return the last algorithm's output. That's because
302.     # the output only matters when a single algorithm is processed; the case
303.     # `algorithm_index==-1` (meaning all algorithms should be processed)
304.     # is used only to init parameters.
305.     accum_mp_state = jax.tree_util.tree_map(
306.         lambda init, tail: jnp.concatenate([init[None], tail], axis=0),
307.         lean_mp_state, accum_mp_state)
308. 
309.     def invert(d):
310.       """Dict of lists -> list of dicts."""
311.       if d:
312.         return [dict(zip(d, i)) for i in zip(*d.values())]
313. 
314.     if return_all_outputs:
315.       output_preds = {k: jnp.stack(v)
316.                       for k, v in accum_mp_state.output_preds.items()}
317.     else:
318.       output_preds = output_mp_state.output_preds
319.     hint_preds = invert(accum_mp_state.hint_preds)
320.

493.             functools.partial(eval_model.predict, algorithm_index=algo_idx),
494.             val_sample_counts[algo_idx],
495.             new_rng_key,
496.             extras=common_extras)
497.         logging.info('(val) algo %s step %d: %s',
498.                      FLAGS.algorithms[algo_idx], step, val_stats)
499.         val_scores[algo_idx] = val_stats['score']
500. 
501.       next_eval += FLAGS.eval_every
502. 
503.       # If best total score, update best checkpoint.
504.       # Also save a best checkpoint on the first step.
505.       msg = (f'best avg val score was '
506.              f'{best_score/len(FLAGS.algorithms):.3f}, '
507.              f'current avg val score is {np.mean(val_scores):.3f}, '
508.              f'val scores are: ')
509.       msg += ', '.join(
510.           ['%s: %.3f' % (x, y) for (x, y) in zip(FLAGS.algorithms, val_scores)])
511.       if (sum(val_scores) > best_score) or step == 0:
512.         best_score = sum(val_scores)
513.         logging.info('Checkpointing best model, %s', msg)
514.         train_model.save_model('best.pkl')
515.       else:
516.         logging.info('Not saving new best model, %s', msg)
517. 
518.     step += 1
519.     length_idx = (length_idx + 1) % len(train_lengths)
520. 
521.   logging.info('Restoring best model from checkpoint...')
522.   eval_model.restore_model('best.pkl', only_load_processor=False)
523. 
524.   for algo_idx in range(len(train_samplers)):
525.     common_extras = {'examples_seen': current_train_items[algo_idx],
526.                      'step': step,
527.                      'algorithm': FLAGS.algorithms[algo_idx]}
528. 
529.     new_rng_key, rng_key = jax.random.split(rng_key)
530.     test_stats = collect_and_eval(
531.         test_samplers[algo_idx],
532.         functools.partial(eval_model.predict, algorithm_index=algo_idx),
533.         test_sample_counts[algo_idx],
534.         new_rng_key,
535.         extras=common_extras)
536.     logging.info('(test) algo %s : %s', FLAGS.algorithms[algo_idx], test_stats)
537. 
538.   logging.info('Done!')
539. 
540. 
541. if __name__ == '__main__':
542.   app.run(main)
543.
```

1. # THIS REPOSITORY

5. ## Branches that matter:

16. !python -m clrs.examples.run --train_steps 10000 --algorithms dfs --hint_mode none --results_df True --save_df True --save_model_to_file True --NSE 25 --filename fourth16 --test_length 16
17. !python -m clrs.examples.run --train_steps 10000 --algorithms dfs --hint_mode none --results_df True --save_df True --save_model_to_file True --NSE 25 --filename fifth16 --test_length 16
18. ```

28. - `results/viz.ipynb` lets you recreate the figures from `.csv` files

30. 
31. Tips navigating CLRS
32. - Use an editor that quickly lets you find a function's definition with a keyboard shortcut, otherwise tracing prediction through baselines, nets, etc... is time consuming
33. - `run.py` sets up `samplers` which make problem instances (e.g. graphs for DFS).
34.   - problem instances live inside named tuples:
35.     - inputs in `feedback.features.inputs` (e.g. Adjacency matrix and Start node)
36.     - labels inside `feedback.features.outputs` (e.g. Correct DFS tree)
37.     - hints inside `feedback.features.hints` 
38. 
39. - Networks predict on `feedback.features.inputs`
40. - Loss is computed by comparing NN output to `feedback.features.outputs`
41.

49. 
50. # The CLRS Algorithmic Reasoning Benchmark
51. 
52. Learning representations of algorithms is an emerging area of machine learning,
53. seeking to bridge concepts from neural networks with classical algorithms. The
54. CLRS Algorithmic Reasoning Benchmark (CLRS) consolidates and extends previous
55. work toward evaluation algorithmic reasoning by providing a suite of
56. implementations of classical algorithms. These algorithms have been selected
57. from the third edition of the standard *Introduction to Algorithms* by Cormen,
58. Leiserson, Rivest and Stein.
59. 
60. ## Getting started
61. 
62. The CLRS Algorithmic Reasoning Benchmark can be installed with pip, either from
63. PyPI:
64. 
65. ```shell
66. pip install dm-clrs
67. ```
68. 
69. or directly from GitHub (updated more frequently):
70. 
71. ```shell
72. pip install git+git://github.com/deepmind/clrs.git
73. ```
74. 
75. You may prefer to install it in a virtual environment if any requirements
76. clash with your Python installation:
77. 
78. ```shell
79. python3 -m venv clrs_env
80. source clrs_env/bin/activate
81. pip install git+git://github.com/deepmind/clrs.git
82. ```
83. 
84. Once installed you can run our example baseline model:
85. 
86. ```shell
87. python3 -m clrs.examples.run
88. ```
89. 
90. If this is the first run of the example, the dataset will be downloaded and
91. stored in `--dataset_path` (default '/tmp/CLRS30').
92. Alternatively, you can also download and extract https://storage.googleapis.com/dm-clrs/CLRS30_v1.0.0.tar.gz
93. 
94. ## Algorithms as graphs
95. 
96. CLRS implements the selected algorithms in an idiomatic way, which aligns as
97. closely as possible to the original CLRS 3ed pseudocode. By controlling the
98. input data distribution to conform to the preconditions we are able to
99. automatically generate input/output pairs. We additionally provide trajectories
100. of "hints" that expose the internal state of each algorithm, to both optionally
101. simplify the learning challenge and to distinguish between different algorithms
102. that solve the same overall task (e.g. sorting).
103. 
104. In the most generic sense, algorithms can be seen as manipulating sets of
105. objects, along with any relations between them (which can themselves be
106. decomposed into binary relations). Accordingly, we study all of the algorithms
107. in this benchmark using a graph representation. In the event that objects obey a
108. more strict ordered structure (e.g. arrays or rooted trees), we impose this
109. ordering through inclusion of predecessor links.
110. 
111. ## How it works
112. 
113. For each algorithm, we provide a canonical set of *train*, *eval* and *test*
114. trajectories for benchmarking out-of-distribution generalization.
115. 
116. |       | Trajectories    | Problem Size |
117. |-------|-----------------|--------------|
118. | Train | 1000            | 16           |
119. | Eval  | 32 x multiplier | 16           |
120. | Test  | 32 x multiplier | 64           |
121. 
122. 
123. Here, "problem size" refers to e.g. the length of an array or number of nodes in
124. a graph, depending on the algorithm. "multiplier" is an algorithm-specific
125. factor that increases the number of available *eval* and *test* trajectories
126. to compensate for paucity of evaluation signals. "multiplier" is 1 for all
127. algorithms except:
128. 
129. - Maximum subarray (Kadane), for which "multiplier" is 32.
130. - Quick select, minimum, binary search, string matchers (both naive and KMP),
131. and segment intersection, for which "multiplier" is 64.
132. 
133. The trajectories can be used like so:
134. 
135. ```python
136. train_ds, num_samples, spec = clrs.create_dataset(
137.       folder='/tmp/CLRS30', algorithm='bfs',
138.       split='train', batch_size=32)
139. 
140. for i, feedback in enumerate(train_ds.as_numpy_iterator()):
141.   if i == 0:
142.     model.init(feedback.features, initial_seed)
143.   loss = model.feedback(rng_key, feedback)
144. ```
145. 
146. Here, `feedback` is a `namedtuple` with the following structure:
147. 
148. ```python
149. Feedback = collections.namedtuple('Feedback', ['features', 'outputs'])
150. Features = collections.namedtuple('Features', ['inputs', 'hints', 'lengths'])
151. ```
152. 
153. where the content of `Features` can be used for training and `outputs` is
154. reserved for evaluation. Each field of the tuple is an `ndarray` with a leading
155. batch dimension. Because `hints` are provided for the full algorithm trajectory,
156. these contain an additional time dimension padded up to the maximum length
157. `max(T)` of any trajectory within the dataset. The `lengths` field specifies the
158. true length `t <= max(T)` for each trajectory, which can be used e.g. for loss
159. masking.
160. 
161. The `examples` directory contains a full working Graph Neural Network (GNN)
162. example using JAX and the DeepMind JAX Ecosystem of libraries. It allows
163. training of multiple algorithms on a single processor, as described in
164. ["A Generalist Neural Algorithmic Learner"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.11142).
165. 
166. ## What we provide
167. 
168. ### Algorithms
169. 
170. Our initial CLRS-30 benchmark includes the following 30 algorithms. We aim to
171. support more algorithms in the future.
172. 
173. - Sorting
174.   - Insertion sort
175.   - Bubble sort
176.   - Heapsort (Williams, 1964)
177.   - Quicksort (Hoare, 1962)
178. - Searching
179.   - Minimum
180.   - Binary search
181.   - Quickselect (Hoare, 1961)
182. - Divide and conquer
183.   - Maximum subarray (Kadane's variant) (Bentley, 1984)
184. - Greedy
185.   - Activity selection (Gavril, 1972)
186.   - Task scheduling (Lawler, 1985)
187. - Dynamic programming
188.   - Matrix chain multiplication
189.   - Longest common subsequence
190.   - Optimal binary search tree (Aho et al., 1974)
191. - Graphs
192.   - Depth-first search (Moore, 1959)
193.   - Breadth-first search (Moore, 1959)
194.   - Topological sorting (Knuth, 1973)
195.   - Articulation points
196.   - Bridges
197.   - Kosaraju's strongly connected components algorithm (Aho et al., 1974)
198.   - Kruskal's minimum spanning tree algorithm (Kruskal, 1956)
199.   - Prim's minimum spanning tree algorithm (Prim, 1957)
200.   - Bellman-Ford algorithm for single-source shortest paths (Bellman, 1958)
201.   - Dijkstra's algorithm for single-source shortest paths (Dijkstra et al., 1959)
202.   - Directed acyclic graph single-source shortest paths
203.   - Floyd-Warshall algorithm for all-pairs shortest-paths (Floyd, 1962)
204. - Strings
205.   - Naïve string matching
206.   - Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) string matcher (Knuth et al., 1977)
207. - Geometry
208.   - Segment intersection
209.   - Graham scan convex hull algorithm (Graham, 1972)
210.   - Jarvis' march convex hull algorithm (Jarvis, 1973)
211. 
212. ### Baselines
213. 
214. Models consist of a *processor* and a number of *encoders* and *decoders*.
215. We provide JAX implementations of the following GNN baseline processors:
216. 
217. - Deep Sets (Zaheer et al., NIPS 2017)
218. - End-to-End Memory Networks (Sukhbaatar et al., NIPS 2015)
219. - Graph Attention Networks (Veličković et al., ICLR 2018)
220. - Graph Attention Networks v2 (Brody et al., ICLR 2022)
221. - Message-Passing Neural Networks (Gilmer et al., ICML 2017)
222. - Pointer Graph Networks (Veličković et al., NeurIPS 2020)
223. 
224. If you want to implement a new processor, the easiest way is to add
225. it in the `processors.py` file and make it available through the
226. `get_processor_factory` method there. A processor should have a `__call__`
227. method like this:
228. 
229. ```
230. __call__(self,
231.          node_fts, edge_fts, graph_fts,
232.          adj_mat, hidden,
233.          nb_nodes, batch_size)
234. ```
235. 
236. where `node_fts`, `edge_fts` and `graph_fts` will be float arrays of shape
237. `batch_size` x `nb_nodes` x H, `batch_size` x `nb_nodes` x `nb_nodes` x H,
238. and `batch_size` x H with encoded features for
239. nodes, edges and graph respectively, `adj_mat` a
240. `batch_size` x `nb_nodes` x `nb_nodes` boolean
241. array of connectivity built from hints and inputs, and `hidden` a
242. `batch_size` x `nb_nodes` x H float array with the previous-step outputs
243. of the processor. The method should return a `batch_size` x `nb_nodes` x H
244. float array.
245. 
246. For more fundamentally different baselines, it is necessary to create a new
247. class that extends the Model API (as found within `clrs/_src/model.py`).
248. `clrs/_src/baselines.py` provides one example of how this can be done.
249. 
250. ## Creating your own dataset
251. 
252. We provide a `tensorflow_dataset` generator class in `dataset.py`. This file can
253. be modified to generate different versions of the available algorithms, and it
254. can be built by using `tfds build` after following the installation instructions
255. at https://www.tensorflow.org/datasets.
256. 
257. Alternatively, you can generate samples without going through `tfds` by
258. instantiating samplers with the `build_sampler` method in
259. `clrs/_src/samplers.py`, like so:
260. 
261. ```
262. sampler, spec = clrs.build_sampler(
263.     name='bfs',
264.     seed=42,
265.     num_samples=1000,
266.     length=16)
267. 
268. def _iterate_sampler(batch_size):
269.   while True:
270.     yield sampler.next(batch_size)
271. 
272. for feedback in _iterate_sampler(batch_size=32):
273.   ...
274. 
275. ```
276. 
277. ## Adding new algorithms
278. 
279. Adding a new algorithm to the task suite requires the following steps:
280. 
281. 1. Determine the input/hint/output specification of your algorithm, and include
282. it within the `SPECS` dictionary of `clrs/_src/specs.py`.
283. 2. Implement the desired algorithm in an abstractified form. Examples of this
284. can be found throughout the `clrs/_src/algorithms/` folder.
285.   - Choose appropriate moments within the algorithm’s execution to create probes
286.     that capture the inputs, outputs and all intermediate state (using
287.     the `probing.push` function).
288.   - Once generated, probes must be formatted using the `probing.finalize`
289.     method, and should be returned together with the algorithm output.
290. 3. Implement an appropriate input data sampler for your algorithm,
291. and include it in the `SAMPLERS` dictionary within `clrs/_src/samplers.py`.
292. 
293. Once the algorithm has been added in this way, it can be accessed with the
294. `build_sampler` method, and will also be incorporated to the dataset if
295. regenerated with the generator class in `dataset.py`, as described above.
296. 
297. ## Citation
298. 
299. To cite the CLRS Algorithmic Reasoning Benchmark:
300. 
301. ```latex
302. @article{deepmind2022clrs,
303.   title={The CLRS Algorithmic Reasoning Benchmark},
304.   author={Petar Veli\v{c}kovi\'{c} and Adri\`{a} Puigdom\`{e}nech Badia and
305.     David Budden and Razvan Pascanu and Andrea Banino and Misha Dashevskiy and
306.     Raia Hadsell and Charles Blundell},
307.   journal={arXiv preprint arXiv:2205.15659},
308.   year={2022}
309. }
310. ```
311.
````

</details>

1. ---
2. name: "pdf"

5. 
6. 
7. # PDF Skill
8. 
9. ## When to use
10. - Read or review PDF content where layout and visuals matter.
11. - Create PDFs programmatically with reliable formatting.
12. - Validate final rendering before delivery.
13. 
14. ## Workflow
15. 1. Prefer visual review: render PDF pages to PNGs and inspect them.
16.    - Use `pdftoppm` if available.
17.    - If unavailable, install Poppler or ask the user to review the output locally.
18. 2. Use `reportlab` to generate PDFs when creating new documents.
19. 3. Use `pdfplumber` (or `pypdf`) for text extraction and quick checks; do not rely on it for layout fidelity.
20. 4. After each meaningful update, re-render pages and verify alignment, spacing, and legibility.
21. 
22. ## Temp and output conventions
23. - Use `tmp/pdfs/` for intermediate files; delete when done.
24. - Write final artifacts under `output/pdf/` when working in this repo.
25. - Keep filenames stable and descriptive.
26. 
27. ## Dependencies (install if missing)
28. Prefer `uv` for dependency management.
29. 
30. Python packages:
31. ```
32. uv pip install reportlab pdfplumber pypdf
33. ```
34. If `uv` is unavailable:
35. ```
36. python3 -m pip install reportlab pdfplumber pypdf
37. ```
38. System tools (for rendering):
39. ```
40. # macOS (Homebrew)
41. brew install poppler
42. 
43. # Ubuntu/Debian
44. sudo apt-get install -y poppler-utils
45. ```
46. 
47. If installation isn't possible in this environment, tell the user which dependency is missing and how to install it locally.
48. 
49. ## Environment
50. No required environment variables.
51. 
52. ## Rendering command
53. ```
54. pdftoppm -png $INPUT_PDF $OUTPUT_PREFIX
55. ```
56. 
57. ## Quality expectations
58. - Maintain polished visual design: consistent typography, spacing, margins, and section hierarchy.
59. - Avoid rendering issues: clipped text, overlapping elements, broken tables, black squares, or unreadable glyphs.
60. - Charts, tables, and images must be sharp, aligned, and clearly labeled.
61. - Use ASCII hyphens only. Avoid U+2011 (non-breaking hyphen) and other Unicode dashes.
62. - Citations and references must be human-readable; never leave tool tokens or placeholder strings.
63. 
64. ## Final checks
65. - Do not deliver until the latest PNG inspection shows zero visual or formatting defects.
66. - Confirm headers/footers, page numbering, and section transitions look polished.
67. - Keep intermediate files organized or remove them after final approval.
````

--- PAGE 1 ---
Project Proposal
Extending a Framework for Neural
Algorithmic Reasoning with Multiple
Solutions
Introduction
Neural Algorithmic Reasoning (NAR) is a paradigm that trains neural networks (NNs)
to reproduce the execution of classical algorithms. Canonical NAR models, typically
based on the encode-process-decode (EPD) architecture, usually learn a single trajectory
or output. However, many algorithms included in benchmarks like the CLRS Algorith-
mic Reasoning Benchmark, such as Depth-First Search (DFS) and Bellman-Ford (BF),
naturally admit multiple correct solutions for a given input graph, often arising due to
arbitrary tie-breaking rules.
The paper, Neural Algorithmic Reasoning with Multiple Correct Solutions (Kujawa et
al., 2025), presents a methodology to address this limitation by training an NN to predict
the underlying distribution of possible solutions. This is achieved by generating diverse
training data through randomized tie-breaking during algorithm execution and then em-
ploying stochastic sampling to extract multiple unique and valid solutions from the NN’s
output distribution.
This project is a software engineering implementation focused on extending this multi-
solution NAR framework. The core objective is to integrate the Breadth-First Search
(BFS)algorithmintothissystem,leveragingthesuccessfulimplementationmethodologies
already established for BF and DFS. BFS is a natural candidate as it is a fundamental
graph traversal algorithm included in the CLRS benchmark and, like DFS, frequently
yields multiple correct spanning trees on unweighted graphs.
The work will focus on three major components:
1. Implementing the data generation pipeline for BFS, incorporating randomized tie-
breaking, following the format used in related BF/DFS research.
2. Training a standard NAR model (e.g., a Message-Passing Neural Network (MPNN)
processor) to predict the BFS solution distribution.
1

--- PAGE 2 ---
3. Implementing and evaluating stochastic sampling techniques to reliably extract mul-
tiple unique and valid BFS solutions.
Starting point
This project will build upon the established CLRS framework from the paper The CLRS
Algorithmic Reasoning Benchmark (Veliˇckovi´c et al., 2022), as well as the algorithms
described in the paper Neural Algorithmic Reasoning with Multiple Correct Solutions
(Kujawa et al., 2025).
I am familiar with fundamental algorithms, including graph traversal and shortest path
algorithms (e.g., Bellman-Ford), often used in NAR tasks. However I do not have any
prior experience working with Graph Neural Networks, nor any experience working with
Deep Learning frameworks like PyTorch or JAX.
I have no prior experience implementing the specific randomized data generators or the
multi-solution extraction framework described in the target paper. No code specific to
this project, including GNN architectures or data generators, will be written
prior to the start of the project in Michaelmas.
Core project
The project is structured around adapting the established NAR methodology for BFS
• Data Generation and Solution Space: I will implement an expert policy for BFS
that, when computing the predecessor array (π), uses randomized tie-breaking
when selecting which node to explore next among eligible candidates. These multiple
resultingpredecessorarraysareaggregatedtoproducethesupervisedsignal: aParent
˜
Probability Distribution matrix (P). Thegenerationprocessshouldtargetgraph
sizes consistent with the CLRS-30 benchmark (N ≤ 64).
• NAR Model Implementation: I will train a standard Graph Neural Network
(GNN) model using the EPD framework, in which the processor component is a
Message-Passing Neural Network (MPNN). The model will be trained using super-
ˆ
vised learning to predict the probability distribution P over parent pointers, minimis-
˜
ing cross-entropy or similar loss against the ground-truth distribution P.
• Extracting Multiple Solutions: Extracting candidate predecessor arrays from the
ˆ
predicted distribution P using algorithm-specific stochastic sampling methods, in this
case for BFS.
• Evaluation of Solutions: Rigorously evaluating the diversity and correctness of the
extracted solutions.
Success criteria
The project will be considered a success if the following goals are demonstrably achieved:
2

--- PAGE 3 ---
1. BFS Data Pipeline: A data generation utility for BFS, incorporating randomized
tie-breaking, is successfully implemented and shown to produce valid Parent Proba-
˜
bility Distribution matrices (P) for a representative set of small and medium graphs.
2. NAR Model Training: The MPNN model is successfully trained on the BFS dis-
tribution data.
3. Multiple Solution Sampling: ImplementmethodsforsamplingvalidBFSsolutions
from a parent distribution.
4. Evaluating Solution Validity: Implement a method to evaluate the correctness of
sampled BFS solutions, ensuring they form valid BFS graph traversals.
Possible extensions
• Implementing Other Algorithms: Implement a similar training and evaluation
pipeline for one or more other algorithms from the CLRS benchmark that also admit
multiple solutions, such as Prim’s algorithm for Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) or
Task Scheduling.
This would allow us to further investigate the generality of this multi-solution NAR
framework. In particular this would provide more insight into the extent to which (i)
certain algorithms (such as DFS, as mentioned in the paper) are hard to emulate with
NAR in the first place, and whether (ii) encoding multiple solutions as a probability
distribution can correctly optimise for correct solutions.
• Multi-Task Training: Investigate how training the model on multiple algorithms
(withmultiplesolutions)simultaneously,allowingthenetworktosharerepresentations
across different tasks, could affect its performance.
• Alternative NAR Architecture: Implement the NAR model using a Pointer
Graph Network (PGN) processor, as PGNs have shown competitive generalisation
out-of-distribution compared to MPNNs on CLRS tasks.

1. import numpy as np
2. from clrs._src import dfs_sampling
3. 
4. def sample_bfs_prim(outsOrPreds, s_indices):
5.     """
6.     Samples BFS trees using a Prim-like greedy approach.
7.     
8.     Args:
9.         outsOrPreds: Model outputs containing parent probabilities.
10.         s_indices: List of source node indices for each graph in the batch.
11.         
12.     Returns:
13.         List of parent arrays (pi), one for each graph in the batch.
14.     """
15.     probMatrix_list = dfs_sampling.extract_probMatrices(outsOrPreds)
16.     pi_trees = []
17.     
18.     # Handle case where s_indices might be a single int or list
19.     if isinstance(s_indices, int):
20.         s_indices = [s_indices] * len(probMatrix_list)
21.         
22.     for i, probMatrix in enumerate(probMatrix_list):
23.         s = s_indices[i]
24.         pi = prim_like_sampler(probMatrix, s)
25.         pi_trees.append(pi)
26.         
27.     return pi_trees
28. 
29. def prim_like_sampler(probMatrix, s):
30.     """
31.     Constructs a BFS tree starting from the root, adding nodes that are most likely 
32.     connected to the current tree.
33.     
34.     Args:
35.         probMatrix: N x N matrix where P[i, j] is prob that j is parent of i.
36.         s: Source node index.
37.         
38.     Returns:
39.         pi: Array of length N, where pi[i] is the parent of i.
40.     """
41.     num_nodes = probMatrix.shape[0]
42.     pi = np.full(num_nodes, -1, dtype=int) # -1 indicates not yet processed/no parent
43.     pi[s] = s
44.     
45.     processed = {s}
46.     remaining = set(range(num_nodes)) - {s}
47.     
48.     # To optimize, we could maintain scores, but N is likely small (<= 64 usually in CLRS)
49.     # So recomputing sum might be fast enough.
50.     
51.     while remaining:
52.         best_v = -1
53.         best_score = -1.0
54.         
55.         # Find v in remaining with highest prob of attaching to processed set
56.         # score(v) = sum_{u in processed} P(parent(v) = u)
57.         for v in remaining:
58.             # probMatrix[v, u] is prob that u is parent of v.
59.             # We sum over u in processed.
60.             score = sum(probMatrix[v, u] for u in processed)
61.             
62.             if score > best_score:
63.                 best_score = score
64.                 best_v = v
65.         
66.         if best_v == -1:
67.             # This happens if remaining nodes have 0 prob of connecting to processed nodes
68.             # (disconnected graph components). 
69.             # We just pick one arbitrarily or handle it?
70.             # For BFS, disconnected nodes typically point to themselves or have 0 parent in some representations.
71.             # Here, let's just pick the first one and attach it to itself (or closest processed if any non-zero).
72.             best_v = list(remaining)[0]
73.             # If score is 0, it means no connection.
74.             # We'll just process it to avoid infinite loop.
75.             
76.         # Sample parent for best_v from processed set
77.         # Probabilities are P(parent(best_v) = u) for u in processed
78.         # We need to normalize these to sum to 1.
79.         
80.         candidate_parents = list(processed)
```

17.     for i in preds: # de-listify into dict, happens twice
18.         distlist = i["pi"].data
19.         for prob in distlist:
20.             amax = np.argmax(prob, axis=1)

25. def sample_argmax_listofdatapoint(outputs):

28.     for i in outputs: #de-listify into datapoint
29.         distlist = i.data
30.         for prob in distlist:
31.             amax = np.argmax(prob, axis=1)
32.             #print(amax)

36. def sample_random_list(outsOrPreds):
37.     '''
38. 
39.     Args:
40.         outsOrPreds: nasty nasty nested lists & dicts, eventually unpacked to probMatrices
41. 
42.     Returns:
43.         trees: a list of dummy "trees" generated by picking a random parent for each vertex
44. 
45.     '''
46.     trees = []
47.     rng = np.random.default_rng()
48.     #breakpoint()
49.     for i in outsOrPreds:
50.         if type(i) == type({}):
51.             distlist = i["pi"].data
52.         else:
53.             distlist = i.data
54.         for probMatrix in distlist:
55.             pi = []
56.             for row in probMatrix:
57.                 pi.append(rng.integers(len(row)))
58.             trees.append(pi)
59.             #breakpoint()
60.     return trees
61.

65. def single_sample_upwards(probMatrix):
66.     '''copy-pasted brain from def sample_upwards'''
67.     probMatrix = np.array(probMatrix)  # deepcopy to numpy so mutable
68. 
69.     # sort by leafiness
70.     leafiness = np.asarray(leafinessSort(probMatrix))  # shallowcopy jax array to numpy array so no problems indexing
71. 
72.     # grab most leafy, find its parent, continue till already-discovered (self-parent or prev. iter).
73.     pi = np.full(len(probMatrix), np.inf)
74.     while sum(leafiness) > -len(leafiness):
75.         altered_ProbMatrix = rowWiseProb(probMatrix)
76.         leaf = leafiness[leafiness != -1][0]
77.         # sample the leafs parent
78.         parent = chooseUniformly(altered_ProbMatrix[leaf])
79.         pi[leaf] = parent  # FIXME sometimes index error
80.         leafiness[leaf] = -1

54. def BF_collect_and_eval(sampler, predict_fn, sample_count, rng_key, extras, filename='bf_accuracy', vd_flag=True, NSE = 100):
55.     """Collect batches of output and hint preds and evaluate them."""
56.     processed_samples = 0
57.     preds = []
58.     outputs = []
59.     As = []
60.     source_nodes = []
61.     while processed_samples < sample_count:
62.         feedback = next(sampler)
63.         batch_size = feedback.outputs[0].data.shape[0]
64.         outputs.append(feedback.outputs)
65.         new_rng_key, rng_key = jax.random.split(rng_key)
66.         cur_preds, _ = predict_fn(new_rng_key, feedback.features)
67.         preds.append(cur_preds)
68.         processed_samples += batch_size
69.         As.append(feedback[0][0][2].data)
70.         source_nodes.append(
71.             np.argmax(feedback[0][0][1].data, axis=1))  # todo checkme. feedback[0][0][1] is 's', .data gives array
72.     outputs = _concat(outputs, axis=0)
73.     As = _concat(As, axis=0)  # concatenate batches
74.     source_nodes = _concat(source_nodes, axis=0)
75.     # breakpoint()
76.     preds = _concat(preds, axis=0)
77.     out = clrs.evaluate(outputs, preds)
78. 
79.     #breakpoint()
80.     if vd_flag:
81.         print('log_exp.py, vd_flag working')

83.         #truncate to just 10 graph

92.         plot_n_unique_by_n_extracted(dataframes, len(As[0]))
93.         df, _, _ = validate_distributions(As=As_vd, Ss=source_nodes_vd, outsOrPreds=[preds_vd], numSolsExtracting=NSE,

385. def bfs_multi(A: _Array, s: int, seed: int, deterministic=False) -> _Out:
386.   """Multiple solution breadth-first search."""
387.   rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)
388. 
389.   chex.assert_rank(A, 2)
390.   probeslist = []
391.   pies = []
392. 
393.   if deterministic:
394.     NUM_SOLUTIONS = 1
395.   else: 
396.     NUM_SOLUTIONS = 20
397. 
398.   for i in range(NUM_SOLUTIONS):
399.     probes = probing.initialize(specs.SPECS['bfs_multi'])
400. 
401.     A_pos = np.arange(A.shape[0])
402. 
403.     probing.push(
404.         probes,
405.         specs.Stage.INPUT,
406.         next_probe={
407.             'pos': np.copy(A_pos) * 1.0 / A.shape[0],
408.             's': probing.mask_one(s, A.shape[0]),
409.             'A': np.copy(A),
410.             'adj': probing.graph(np.copy(A))
411.         })
412. 
413.     reach = np.zeros(A.shape[0])
414.     pi = np.arange(A.shape[0])
415.     reach[s] = 1
416.     while True:
417.       prev_reach = np.copy(reach)
418.       probing.push(
419.           probes,
420.           specs.Stage.HINT,
421.           next_probe={
422.               'reach_h': np.copy(prev_reach),
423.               'pi_h': np.copy(pi)
424.           })
425.       
426.       # Randomise order of sources (reached nodes) to generate different valid BFS trees
427.       # All nodes in prev_reach are at the same distance from root, so any can be a valid parent
428.       # Shuffling determines which one "claims" a child first when multiple are valid
429.       n = A.shape[0]
430.       sources = np.where(prev_reach == 1)[0]
431.       if deterministic:
432.         shuffled_sources = sources
433.       else:
434.         shuffled_sources = np.copy(sources)
435.         rng.shuffle(shuffled_sources)
436.       for src in shuffled_sources:
437.         for j in range(n):
438.           if A[src, j] > 0:
439.             if pi[j] == j and j != s:
440.               pi[j] = src
441.             reach[j] = 1
442.       if np.all(reach == prev_reach):
443.         break
444. 
445.     probing.push(probes, specs.Stage.OUTPUT, next_probe={'pi': np.copy(pi)})
446.     probing.finalize(probes)
447. 
448.     pies.append(pi)
449.     probeslist.append(probes)
450. 
451.   ### copied from DFS CODE
452.   # build adj matrix of "is i a parent of j in any pi", sums and divides.
453.   adjs = []
454.   for i in range(NUM_SOLUTIONS):
455.       adj = np.zeros(A.shape)
456.       for j in range(len(pies[0])):  # what's the parent of j?
457.           #breakpoint()
458.           adj[j, pies[i][j]] = 1  # at row j, put 1 in the column corresponding to parent
459.       adjs.append(adj)
460.   parent_dist = sum(adjs) / NUM_SOLUTIONS
461.   # parent_dist = sp.special.logit(parent_dist)
462.   # print(probes)
463.   # print(parent_dist)
464.   probeslist[0]['output']['node']['pi']['data'] = parent_dist
465. 
466.   #breakpoint()
467.   ## CHECK THE PUSHING!
468.   return parent_dist, probeslist[0]

class DfsMultiSampler(Sampler):
  """DFS sampler that passes seed for multi-solution generation."""
  
  def _sample_data(
      self, 
      length: int, 
      p: Tuple[float, ...] = (0.5,),
    ):
      graph = self._random_er_graph(
          nb_nodes=length, p=self._rng.choice(p),
          directed=True, acyclic=False, weighted=False)
      
      # Add deterministic seed for algorithm
      sub_seed = self._rng.randint(0, 2**31)
      
      return [graph, sub_seed]  # ← Extra parameter

    graph = self._random_er_graph(
        nb_nodes=length, p=self._rng.choice(p),
        directed=False, acyclic=False, weighted=False)
    source_node = self._rng.choice(length)

30. def fuse_perm_and_mask(perm: probing.DataPoint,
31.                        mask: probing.DataPoint) -> probing.DataPoint:
32.   """Replace permutation pointers active in the mask with self-pointers.
33. 
34.   Args:
35.     perm: a node permutation_pointer; data shape is expected to be
36.       [..., N, N], and ideally one-hot over the last two dimensions, although
37.       this method does not check for one-hotness.
38.     mask: a mask_one over nodes; data shape is expected to be
39.       [..., N], and ideally one-hot over the last dimension, although
40.       this method does not check for one-hotness.
41.   Returns:
42.     A node pointer with shape [..., N].
43.   """
44.   assert perm.type_ == specs.Type.PERMUTATION_POINTER
45.   assert perm.location == specs.Location.NODE
46.   assert mask.name == perm.name + '_mask'
47.   assert mask.type_ == specs.Type.MASK_ONE
48.   assert mask.location == specs.Location.NODE
49.   assert perm.data.shape[-1] == perm.data.shape[-2]
50.   assert perm.data.shape[:-1] == mask.data.shape
51.   data = np.where(mask.data > 0.5,
52.                   np.arange(perm.data.shape[-1]),  # self-pointers
53.                   np.argmax(perm.data, axis=-1))   # original pointers
54.   return probing.DataPoint(name=perm.name,
55.                            type_=specs.Type.POINTER,
56.                            location=perm.location,
57.                            data=data)
58. 
59. 
60. def _reduce_permutations_tuple(
61.     targets: Tuple[probing.DataPoint, ...]) -> Tuple[probing.DataPoint, ...]:
62.   """Reduce node pointer + mask_one permutation to just node pointer."""
63.   out_targets = []
64.   n_perms = 0
65.   i = 0
66.   while i < len(targets):
67.     truth = targets[i]
68.     #hi
69.     #print('in evalutation, truth=', truth)
70.     #print(truth.data)
71.     if truth.type_ != specs.Type.PERMUTATION_POINTER:
72.       out_targets.append(truth)
73.       i += 1
74.       continue
75.     truth_mask = targets[i + 1]
76.     out_targets.append(fuse_perm_and_mask(truth, truth_mask))
77.     i += 2
78.     n_perms += 1
79. 
80.   assert len(out_targets) == len(targets) - n_perms

# CLRS Multi-Solution Contribution Analysis

## PROPOSAL CONTRIBUTION SUMMARY

### Intended Architecture (from proposal.pdf)

The project proposes extending the Neural Algorithmic Reasoning (NAR) framework to handle **multiple correct solutions** for algorithms where ambiguity arises from tie-breaking rules. The core research problem:
- **Baseline limitation**: Canonical NAR models train on single-solution trajectories, losing solution diversity
- **Motivation**: Algorithms like DFS, Bellman-Ford (BF), and BFS naturally admit multiple valid solutions
- **Solution approach**: Train models to predict solution distributions rather than single outputs

### Three-Part Architecture:
1. **Data Generation Pipeline**: Generate diverse solutions via randomized tie-breaking in algorithm implementations
2. **NAR Model Training**: Train models using KL-divergence loss on parent probability distributions
3. **Solution Extraction**: Implement stochastic sampling methods to extract multiple unique valid solutions

### Part II Contributions (Explicitly Claimed):

From proposal pages 1-2:
1. **BFS Data Pipeline Implementation**
   - Generate parent probability distributions (P̃) with randomized tie-breaking
   - Target graph sizes consistent with CLRS-30 (N ≤ 64)

2. **MPNN-based NAR Model Training**
   - Train using encode-process-decode architecture
   - Cross-entropy/KL-divergence loss minimization
   
3. **Multiple Solution Extraction**
   - Stochastic sampling methods for BFS (beyond argmax)
   - Algorithm-specific solution sampling techniques

4. **Solution Evaluation**
   - Correctness validation (BFS tree verification)
   - Diversity metrics

### Possible Extensions (Not Core):
- Other multi-solution algorithms (Prim's, Task Scheduling)
- Multi-task training
- PGN processor alternative

---

## BASELINE CLRS/NAR COMPONENTS (Inherited)

### From CLRS Benchmark (Veličković et al., 2022):
- **Core architecture**: Encode-Process-Decode (EPD) framework
- **30 algorithms** including DFS, BFS, Bellman-Ford, sorting, etc.
- **GNN processors**: MPNN, GAT, PGN, Deep Sets, E2E Memory Networks
- **Standard dataset generation**: Problem samplers for train/eval/test splits
- **Baselines**: Complete training and evaluation pipeline

### From NAR Multiple Solutions Paper (Kujawa et al., 2025):
- **Methodology**: Multi-run algorithm execution with randomized tie-breaking
- **DFS multi-solution**: Already fully implemented (dfs_multi, dfs_sampling, etc.)
- **Bellman-Ford multi-solution**: Already fully implemented (bf_*, BF_beamsearch, etc.)
- **Solution sampling framework**: Established patterns (argmax, random, upwards sampling)

## **1. PROPOSAL CONTRIBUTION SUMMARY**

### Intended Architecture & Research Plan

The proposal addresses a **fundamental NAR limitation**: canonical neural algorithmic reasoners train on single-solution trajectories, but many CLRS algorithms (DFS, BFS, Bellman-Ford) admit multiple equally-valid solutions due to arbitrary tie-breaking.

**Three-Part Framework:**
1. **Data Generation**: Run algorithms 20× with randomized tie-breaking to generate diverse solutions; aggregate into parent probability distributions P̃
2. **NAR Training**: Train MPNN processor to predict P̃ using KL-divergence loss on parent-pointer matrices
3. **Solution Extraction**: Implement stochastic sampling methods (Upwards, Argmax, Random, Beam Search) to extract multiple unique valid solutions from predicted distributions

**Success Criteria (from proposal, pages 2-3):**
- BFS data pipeline with randomized tie-breaking producing valid probability matrices
- MPNN model training on BFS distribution data
- Multiple solution sampling implementation
- Solution validity evaluation (tree structure verification)

733. def _batch_io(traj_io: Trajectories) -> Trajectory:
734.   """Batches a trajectory of input/output samples along the time axis per probe.
735. 
736.   Args:
737.     traj_io:  An i/o trajectory of `DataPoint`s indexed by time then probe.
738. 
739.   Returns:
740.     A |num probes| list of `DataPoint`s with the time axis stacked into `data`.
741.   """
742. 
743.   assert traj_io  # non-empty
744.   for sample_io in traj_io:
745.     for i, dp in enumerate(sample_io):
746.       assert dp.data.shape[0] == 1  # batching axis
747.       assert traj_io[0][i].name == dp.name
748. 
749.   return jax.tree_util.tree_map(lambda *x: np.concatenate(x), *traj_io)
